title: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து
theme: Invocation of God (கடவுள் வாழ்த்து): Siva, often named Nandi, is one and many, beyond the gods who cannot measure him and without equal, yet near to those who love him; the chapter urges praise in any form and promises that grace answers it.
structure_note: The chapter opens with a number verse (1) and a declaration of what the poet will sing (2). Verses 5 to 23 set Siva above and beyond the gods, the elements and the worlds; from about 24 the stress shifts to praise, worship and its fruit, often in the refrain 'praise him, and if you praise...' (25, 26, 35, 36, 39). It closes on the poet's own worship (44, 48, 50) and on crossing beyond pasu and pasam (49).
source_issues: 14: line 1 reads கடந்துநினின் றான், a misprint for கடந்துநின் றான்.
23: line 1 reads வன்னிககு, a misprint for வன்னிக்கு; the line's legend is obscure.
26: line 3 reads கடந்துநின் றாம் (we stood beyond), probably for கடந்துநின் றான் as in 14.
30: line 2 reads தானினறு, a misprint for தான்நின்று.
49: line 2 reads பாசததுஒருங்க, a misprint for பாசத்து ஒருங்க, and line 4 கடநது for கடந்து.
16, 17, 19, 23, 35, 40 and 43 have lines too obscure to read with confidence and may be corrupt.

reading: He is one; he is two with his sweet grace; he stood within three, knew four, conquered five, spread out as six, went up beyond seven, and remains, knowing eight.
nuance: The verse is a count from one to eight and names almost none of what is counted. Traditionally: two as Siva with Shakti (his grace), three as the three gods or the three gunas, four as the Vedas, five as the senses, six as the six adhvas or the Vedangas, seven as the worlds above, eight as the eight qualities or the eightfold form. Only ஐந்து வென்றனன் (conquered five) and இன்னருள் (sweet grace) are fairly secure.

reading: Praising him, I tell of the pure one in whom dear life abides, the lord of the four directions and of the good lady, who became king even over the southern quarter by kicking Death.
nuance: கூற்றுதைத்தான் recalls the legend of Siva kicking Yama to save Markandeya. The south is Yama's direction, which is why தென் திசைக்கொரு வேந்தன் is taken this way; மேற்றிசைக்குள் (within the western, or the upper, quarter) is unclear.

reading: I enter in and meditate and praise every day the Supreme who stands alike in all, whom the undying gods hail as the naked one, and whom even those who stand at his side do not know.
nuance: நக்கன் (the naked one) is a name of Siva as the bare ascetic. ஒக்க நின்றான் may mean 'stands equally in everything' or 'stands together' (with Shakti). The verse sets those near him who fail to know him against the poet who enters within (புக்கு நின்று).

reading: Bowing and praising day and night the truth of those on the wide earth, the seed of the cosmos, who sent me into refuge with him, I stood free of darkness in the very place of strife.
nuance: போதவிட்டான் can be 'sent me forth' or, from போதம் (knowledge), 'made me understand'. இருள் (darkness) is traditionally the soul's root impurity (anava). இகலிடம், the place of strife, is taken as this world of birth.

reading: Search as you may, there is no god equal to Siva and no one here like him; the lotus-bearer with burning matted hair flashes with golden light beyond the worlds.
nuance: The claim is exclusive: not that Siva is highest among gods but that none compares. தாமரையான் is unusual for Siva and may mean one who wears the lotus, or one whose feet are lotuses.

reading: Apart from him there are no gods, no hard penance, nothing the three can achieve, and I know no way to enter the city.
nuance: The three (மூவர்) are usually Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra. ஊர் புகுமாறு, the way to enter the city, is traditionally taken as reaching release or Siva's world; a plain reading is possible but makes little sense here.

reading: He is elder to the three who are ancient alike, the chief with nothing like him; call him father and he is father too, the one of knowledge who shines like gold.
nuance: போதகத்தான் is taken as the one of knowledge (போதகம்), though போதகம் can also mean a young elephant. தன்னை அப்பா எனில் அப்பனுமாய் உளன: he becomes to the worshipper what the worshipper calls him.

reading: He is hotter than fire and cooler than water, yet no one knows the Lord's grace; far off, yet near to those who love well, the one with hanging matted hair is kinder than a mother.
nuance: சேயினும் நல்லன் can mean 'better than a child' or, with சேய் as 'distant', 'far beyond'; the second pairs with அணியன் (near). The opposites (hot and cool, far and near) say that grace is unknown not because it is hidden but because it is both at once.

reading: The one who sits with matted hair shining behind him like twisted gold is named Nandi; he is our Lord whom I worship, and there is none whom he worships.
nuance: Nandi here is a name of Siva, as throughout the chapter; Tirumular also calls his teacher Nandi, and the two are not always easy to separate.

reading: He himself bears the great earth and stands as the sky; he is the burning fire, the sun and the moon; he stands as the lady who pours rain; he is the great mountain and the cool sea.
nuance: தானே opens every line: he is these things, not only their maker. மழைபொழி தையல் (the rain-pouring lady) is taken as Shakti, so his consort too is a form of him.

reading: Look at our First One near and around, and there is no great god to compare; the end of every effort is there too; the great Nandi is the rain-pouring cloud.
nuance: முயலும் முயலில் முடிவும் மற்றாங்கே is compressed: the goal of all striving is in him. அயலும் புடையும் (near and around) may also mean other gods and those beside him.

reading: While the god with the eye in his forehead remains in one love, many say countless gods have died; those who go to the earth and those who reach the sky do not know that he is the Lord.
nuance: The contrast is between the gods who die and Siva who stays. ஒரு காதலின் நிற்க (stays in one love, or one desire) is unclear: perhaps his unchanging love for souls.

reading: Vishnu who measured the earth, Brahma of the flower and the other gods, even measuring with thought, still cannot conceive the Lord; no one has measured above him who measured the sky; measured by the eye, he stands beyond everything.
nuance: The verse plays on அளத்தல் (measuring) and recalls the legend of the column of fire whose top and bottom Brahma and Vishnu could not find. விண்ணளந்தான் may be Vishnu again (who measured the sky) or Siva.

reading: He stands beyond the lotus-born one, beyond our dark sea-coloured Mayan, beyond even what lies past them; the Lord stands beyond everywhere and stands seeing all.
nuance: கடந்துநின்றான் (stood beyond) opens every line. The last words, கண்டுநின்றான், balance transcendence with presence: beyond all, he still watches all.

reading: As the First and as Hara, as the transformer standing within the body, he spread and filled and remained; as the light of grace and as justice in a nature that never shrinks, he stands eternal.
nuance: வேதி is taken as the one who transforms (as alchemy changes metal), or as the Vedic one; the first fits உடலுள் நின்ற, within the body. The verse places the Lord in the body as well as beyond the world, a theme the later tantras develop.

reading: The immortals and the gods, delighting in the one with konrai in his matted hair who shares half his body with the bright-browed lady, practise his qualities.
nuance: கோது குலாவிய recurs in lines 1 and 4 and is obscure: கோது can mean dross, fault or a flower's sheath, so the last line may say the gods, for all their worship, still cling to faults. யாது குலாவி (delighting in what?) may be a question.

reading: Even if asafoetida and the like are boiled together with it, musk's scent prevails; in the same way, even if one mixes with the gods of many lands and thinks of one as god, nothing equals kinship with the Lord.
nuance: காயம் is read as asafoetida, set against கத்தூரி (musk); it can also mean the body. இரண்டும் and மாயம் are hard to fit, and the simile's point (the stronger scent wins) is a reading.

reading: Seeing the full penance of the king of Alaka, our Lord made him overlord and lord of wealth, and said: if you cherish that lordship and make it prosper, take this lordship.
nuance: The king of Alaka is Kubera, made lord of wealth by Siva for his penance. The speech in the last two lines is compressed and its sense uncertain.

reading: The one of ancient wisdom, who made the seven groves fragrant with cardamom an ancient seat, seeing the true penance of the one he made lord, dwells there as that seat.
nuance: The verse continues 18 (இதுபதி) and plays on பதி as lord and as place. விதுபதி may be the moon's lord or a misreading; who did the penance and which seat is meant are unclear.

reading: If you seek the path of virtue where the Lord dwells who first created death and birth, thunder and its roar are the Lord's form, and it is the mountain of fragrant flowers.
nuance: The second half is obscure. கடிமலர்க் குன்ற மலை may be Kailasa or a particular hill; the thunder as his form may echo the rain imagery of 10 and 11.

reading: Praise the king who tore the forest elephant so that it screamed, the One who ends the flawed birth of Vishnu dark as a great cloud, of Brahma and of the gods, and you may join him.
nuance: The elephant is the demon Siva flayed (Gajasura). ஊனப் பிறவி (flawed, or fleshly, birth) puts even the high gods inside the round of births from which only Siva frees.

reading: The good lord of the land of maya, who rises within the mind, knows what one thinks; yet people do not think of him and say 'the Lord has no love for me', while the Lord stands caring for those who would be saved.
nuance: பிழைக்க நின்றார் can be 'those who stand to be saved' or 'those who stand in error'; on the second reading, his care reaches even the wrongdoers. The complaint that God has no love is answered: it is people who do not think of him.

reading: Do not say there is no Lord: the mighty one, just Lord who made the elephant stop at his word, first of the gods, gives grace by night and day.
nuance: The first line (வன்னிக்கு இறையிடை வாரணம்) refers to a legend I can't identify; வன்னி may be fire or the vanni tree. இல்லென வேண்டா, 'don't say he is not', is plain.

reading: Praise and laud the holy one's feet and grow clear; the wealth is always Siva's feet; he stays firm in the way of those who have turned back the mind that was deluded.
nuance: The middle is compressed: 'wealth is Siva's feet' revalues செல்வம். ஆற்றியதென்று மயலுற்ற சிந்தை may be the mind deluded by thinking it has achieved something.

reading: Worship the unborn, deathless, never-departing one, the bearer of the bow, great in grace, who gives joy to all; if you worship, the never-forgetting one becomes for you an undying greatness.
nuance: A string of -இலி names (பிறப்பிலி, இறப்பிலி, துறப்பிலி, மறப்பிலி: without birth, death, leaving, forgetting). மாயா விருத்தம் is unclear: 'unperishing greatness' or 'the state free of maya'.

reading: Worship the one who follows you; if you worship, he spreads through all the earth, stands beyond, above the lotus flower, and dwelling with him is the merit of his feet.
nuance: தொடர்ந்துநின்றான் (who follows, or stays with, the soul) is a mark of grace. கடந்துநின்றாம் (we stood beyond) is probably கடந்துநின்றான் (he stood beyond), as in 14; the lotus may be Brahma's or the heart's.

reading: Those who bow daily to Nandi, saying 'the grace of the endless Lord with the bright lotus face, fit to be called the meeting-point, is for us', he enters and stays within their minds.
nuance: சந்தி (twilight, or a junction) is unclear; it may be the dawn-and-dusk hour of worship. The verse's claim is plain: he enters the minds of those who bow to him.

reading: He stands in accord and has become everything; he stands apart and has become before and behind; the lord of Amaravati stands withered; to those who stand bowing he is a companion on the way.
nuance: இணங்கி / பிணங்கி (agreeing, opposing) give the Lord both relations to the world. The lord of Amaravati is Indra; உணங்கி நின்றான் may say Indra stands humbled before Siva, or it may describe Siva, which is harder to make sense of.

reading: Stand where I can see you: who else is kin to me, your servant? I will not hold back in shame from embracing you. He has settled as the linchpin in the minds of devotees whose nature never bends.
nuance: The first two lines address the Lord directly, the last two speak of him. ஆணி (nail, linchpin, or the finest gold) makes him what holds the devotee's mind in place.

reading: Some hesitate, wondering whether the Lord, like rain calling from the sky, will call them from where he stands; as the cow stands and calls, I stand and call my Nandi, seeking knowledge.
nuance: The two images are set against each other: waiting to be called down from above, and calling out oneself as a cow lows for its calf (or a calf for its mother; ஆன் can be either). The poet calls ஞானம் கருதி, wanting knowledge, not reward.

reading: He is the same on earth, in the sky, in the heavens and in the Veda; for him who took to singing sweet music in melody, I stood in my eye and loved.
nuance: கண்ணகத்தே நின்று can be read as the Lord standing within the eye or the poet loving with his whole sight. Sengalvaraya notes the same phrase in Tiruvasagam (Tiruppalliyezhuchi 9).

reading: The lord of the gods, our lord, who fills the ten directions and strides across the seven worlds of spreading water: no one knows his nature, and to praise the all-pervading lord becomes a song of grace.
nuance: பிரான் closes each half-line. The last line may mean that singing of him is itself grace, or that he is reached through songs of grace.

reading: Of old this world had many lords; people perform many rites and do not see the one truth; even those who can recite many praises and hymns lack understanding and wither within.
nuance: A check on the chapter's own call to praise: hymns and rites without understanding (மதி) leave the heart withered. பதிபல may be many gods or many cities and shrines; விதி பல may be rules or rites.

reading: Like the scent the sandal-fragrant yak-tail fan carries, the true way the king gave the gods and his thousand names, like a full flame, I praise whether going or sitting.
nuance: The simile is hard to fix: the scent may be the true way, which spreads like the fan's fragrance, or the names. போந்தும் இருந்தும் (going and staying) means at all times.

reading: Praise the Lord who is the way when no way avails; praise and laud him, and if you laud him he will change you, through the eight directions with west and east, and set you dancing so.
nuance: ஆற்றுகிலா வழி (the way for those unable to cope, or the way one cannot achieve oneself) and the last two lines are obscure. மாற்றுவன் may be 'transform you' or 'turn you about'; ஆட்டவுமாம் may speak of the soul made to dance as Siva dances.

reading: Praise in whatever way you can the father, Nandi, the nectar one never tires of, the peerless giver, the first of the aeon; if you praise him, you can win the Lord's grace in that same measure.
nuance: எப்பரிசாயினும் ... அப்பரிசு: grace answers praise in kind and measure. The verse lowers the bar for worship: any form will do.

reading: I too stand and praise Nandi every day; he too stands, his body like flame; like the moon in the sky he delights within the body and stands in the flesh, and so it breathes with life.
nuance: உயிர்க்கின்றவாறே is read as 'that is how it lives'. The verse puts the Lord in the flesh as the source of its life, which the later tantras develop as the body as temple. The moon image may be yogic.

reading: I will not stop babbling of the great and rare one, of the one whose form is unborn, of our great Nandi, of the one of greatness.
nuance: பிதற்று is raving or babbling, the devotee's speech that does not care how it sounds; repeated at the head of each line, it enacts what it says.

reading: By praising the light within the minds of those able to praise, the holy one, the god who delights there, by bowing to him as our Lord and holding him dear, one can win the Lord's grace.
nuance: The light is already in the minds of those who praise; worship here is turning toward what is within. ஆத்தம் is taken as love or trust.

reading: The Lord's anklet-ringing feet, which the humbled come to seek, are like the light of pure red gold; for those who can praise without hidden guile, he enters and stays and works on the outer frame.
nuance: மறைஞ்சடம் is taken as concealed deceit and புறஞ்சடம் as the outer body, so the last line may mean he transforms or removes the outer body; the second half is obscure.

reading: For those who can praise in a heart tilled like a field the lord of the gods who swallowed the raging poison, the one who shares half his body with the bright-browed lady stays there in accord, like a deer among its herd.
nuance: புனஞ்செய்த நெஞ்சு, the heart made into a cleared field, is a farming image for a mind prepared to receive him; the deer at ease with its kind says he dwells there naturally.

reading: What those who go and praise Hara gain is what the Lord made the crown; even if they come wrapped in maya, the king of the bamboo-shouldered lady becomes one with them.
nuance: நாயகனான் முடி செய்ததுவே நல்கும் is obscure: perhaps the highest state, or the crown he gave others. The point that maya is no bar to praise is fairly clear.

reading: For those who, speaking of Hara's feet, crying and weeping, seek and meditate daily on the feet of the Supreme and can settle there, he fills them, giving his feet in order.
nuance: அரற்றி அழுது (crying out and weeping) is the devotional weeping of the Tamil saints. உரன் அடி செய்து and நிரன் அடி செய்து are obscure; the play on அடி runs through all four lines.

reading: The gods say 'praise' to the pure one's feet, the asuras say it, humans say it; I have set 'praise' to shine within my love.
nuance: Gods, demons and humans alike praise him; what sets the poet apart is not the word but where it is placed, inside love.

reading: This sea-girt world runs only by ordinance, and outside the ordinance there is neither joy nor its opposite; by the way of daily praise, the Lord of light becomes the sun that shows the way to the Lord.
nuance: விதி may be fate, divine ordinance or prescribed rule, and விருத்தம் the contrary of joy or something else. The verse sets the way of ordinance (விதிவழி) against the way of praise (துதிவழி) and the way to the Lord (பதிவழி).

reading: While devotees made worship, thinking 'you of twilight colour, Hara, Siva' and 'you of the first colour, First One, Supreme', the one whose colour is the intellect entered our mind.
nuance: The play on வண்ணம் (colour, form, manner) runs through the verse: the red of evening, the first, and finally புந்தி வண்ணன், one whose form is understanding.

reading: Those who stay in the household are equal to great ascetics; those who keep him in thought stand in his love; but like the kite perched in the palmyra, those who do not think of you have no joy of you.
nuance: The first line read alone equates householders with ascetics; read with the second, it may mean householders who keep the Lord in mind. The kite in the palmyra is traditionally taken as sitting by the fruit and not tasting it, or as perched without settling.

reading: Bowing my head to the lord of the immortals whom devotees extol, thinking of the First One, our father, the Supreme beyond the supreme who gives grace in measure, I stay with him as a lamp that needs no dawn.
nuance: விடியா விளக்கு is a lamp that does not go out at dawn, or one that needs no daybreak; it may describe the Lord or the poet's steady devotion. படியால் may be 'on earth' or 'in measure'.

reading: Those who think of the Lord of pasu and pasam and can gather themselves on the teaching of pasu and pasam will swim the rich sea of sin and reach the shore, passing beyond pasu and pasam.
nuance: பசு பாசம் closes the first half of every line, with நரை, உரை, திரை, கரை before it. Traditionally pasu is the soul and pasam its bonds, under pati the Lord, the three categories of Saiva Siddhanta. நரை (grey, ancient) and திரை (wave) are hard to fit.

reading: Calling him Lord I will wear him and keep him in my heart; I will sing, scatter many flowers, bow and dance, and dancing seek him as the lord of the immortals: this is what I know today.
nuance: The verse lists the acts of worship (wearing, holding, singing, scattering flowers, bowing, dancing, seeking) and ends with the modest claim that this is all he knows today.

title: வேதச் சிறப்பு
theme: The greatness of the Veda (வேதச் சிறப்பு): there is no dharma outside the Veda, the Lord spoke it to show the true reality, and Vedanta teaches the one path that joins the guru's way to Siva's. Yet those who recite it seldom live by its qualities and turn it to gain.
structure_note: Praise of the Veda as the whole of dharma and the way to release (51 to 54), then two verses on those who misuse it (55, 56).
source_issues: 51: line 4 ends வீடுபெற் றார்க்களே, apparently for வீடுபெற்றார்களே.

reading: There is no dharma that leaves out the Veda; all the dharma worth reciting is in it, and the wise, giving up disputation and argument, recited the rich Veda and gained release.
nuance: The verse sets recitation against தர்க்க வாதம் (logic and debate): release comes from reciting the Veda, not from arguing about it. 'All dharma is in the Veda' is the verse's own claim, stated without qualification.

reading: The one who spoke the Veda is not himself a Vedic priest; he spoke it so that Brahma might shine, for the sacrifices of the Vedic people, and to show the true reality.
nuance: The four lines all open வேதம் உரைத்தானும். வேதா is taken as Brahma, and the speaker as the Lord, who gives the Veda without belonging to the priestly order. Line 1 could also mean that merely uttering the Veda does not make one a வேதியன்; the verse allows both.

reading: Within the beautiful Veda whose form is the Rig, rising within the Veda as the feeling that melts and is felt, he is also Kannan, standing as the inner form that the awe-inspiring Vedic seers speak of.
nuance: The rhyme words இருக்கு, உருக்கு, வெருக்கு, கருக்கு drive the verse and blur its syntax. இருக்கு is the Rig Veda; கண்ணன் may be Vishnu or a name of the Lord as the eye (கண்) of the Veda. The point seems to be that the Lord is the inner content of the Veda.

reading: The holy path is to think of the Lord, the great path beyond the sentient and the insentient, and so join the guru's path that is Siva's path; Vedanta teaches this one path as one.
nuance: சித்து அசித்து (the sentient and the insentient) is a standard pair of Siddhanta. The verse makes Vedanta the teacher of Tirumular's own path, guru and Siva together, rather than a rival school.

reading: No one practises the qualities of the great Veda that comes with its six limbs as part of themselves; instead they make it yield other results and then enlarge it into a means of gain.
nuance: ஆறங்கம் are the six auxiliary sciences of the Veda. The verse plays on அங்கம் (limb) four times: கூறங்கமாக (as a part of oneself), வேறங்கமாக (as something else), பேறங்கமாக (as gain). The reading of the last two lines, that they use the Veda for profit, is the plainest, not the only one.

reading: In a land never free of song, music and the dancing of courtesans, those who cannot hold back, who perform sacrifices and desire, keeping no vows, go where wealth is heaped and fall to quarrelling.
nuance: மாட்டாதார் (those unable) has no stated object, and வேட்டு may mean 'having sacrificed' or 'desiring'. In this chapter it is likely aimed at Vedic men who perform rites without the discipline of vows (விரதம்) and chase wealth, but the verse does not name them.

title: ஆகமச் சிறப்பு
theme: The greatness of the Agamas (ஆகமச் சிறப்பு): the Lord gave the Siva Agamas by grace, through a chain from Siva to Nandi; they are past counting, yet without the knowledge the Lord declared they are writing on water. He spoke them in Sanskrit and Tamil alike, and both languages make him known.
structure_note: The Agamas' origin and number (57, 58, 60), their transmission and names (61 to 63), the warning that their number is worthless without knowledge (64), and the two languages of revelation (59, 65, 66).

reading: The twenty-eight Agamas are the rare meaning that the sixty-six, with joined palms, heard from the fearless face of the one who has the dark-bodied woman as half of himself.
nuance: அஞ்சொடு இருபத்துமூன்று (five with twenty-three) gives the traditional count of 28 Saiva Agamas. அஞ்சா முகம் may be 'fearless face' or, punning, அஞ்சு ஆம் முகம், the five faces from which tradition says the Agamas came. Who the sixty-six hearers are the verse does not say.

reading: The Siva Agamas the Lord gives by his grace number twenty-eight crore hundred-thousand; they told the greatness of the Lord of the gods, and I, keeping that meaning in mind, praise it.
nuance: The number is a figure of vastness, not a count. The verse turns at the end to the poet's own task: what he praises is the meaning (அப்பொருள்), not the bulk.

reading: Say that the learned are those who know the intent of what the seers of the eighteen languages say; the eighteen languages of the learned are the way the First of the cosmos told dharma.
nuance: பதினெட்டுப் பாடை is usually taken as the eighteen languages of the land. On that reading the verse makes every language a channel of the Lord's dharma and the learned those who grasp intent rather than words. Whether பதினெட்டும் pairs with பாடையும் or names eighteen other things is unclear.

reading: The divine Agamas the Lord gives by his grace are hard to understand even for the immortals in heaven; counted, they come to seventy crore hundred-thousand, and even that count is writing on water.
nuance: The last line can mean that the number itself is meaningless, or, as 64 states outright, that the Agamas are writing on water for anyone who does not understand them. The number differs from 58 (twenty-eight crore), which suggests both are figures of vastness.

reading: When the Supreme, showing the supreme-beyond, as support of the world, himself spoke the Siva dharma, Nandi, worshipped by the immortals as Hara, became its strength and stood high as the Agama.
nuance: பரம் and பராபரம் are technical terms for the Supreme and what lies beyond it. தரனாய், அரனாய், உரனாகி rhyme and are hard to separate: Nandi may be Siva himself here, or the first receiver who becomes the Agama's support.

reading: The nine Agamas that, from Siva as the Supreme, Shakti, Sadasiva, Mahesa, the Rudra gods, Vishnu, Brahma and the Lord received each from the other, our Nandi received.
nuance: The verse gives a chain of transmission ending in Nandi, Tirumular's own teacher. உவமா and தவமால் பிரமீசர் may divide in other ways, so the exact list of links is not certain. The nine Agamas are named in 63.

reading: The good Agamas he received are Karanam, Kamikam, the noble Viram, the lofty Sinthiyam, Vathulam, Yamalam, Kalottaram, the good Suppiram and Makutam.
nuance: These are names from the traditional list of 28 Agamas (Karana, Kamika, Vira, Cintya, Vatula, Yamala, Kalottara, Suprabheda and Makuta). சுப்பிரம் is taken as Suprabheda.

reading: Though the Siva Agamas the Lord gives by his grace are gathered in countless crores, if one does not know the knowledge the Lord declared, all those crores are writing on water.
nuance: The verse repeats 58's first line and turns it against bulk: the measure of the Agamas is the knowledge (அறிவு) they carry, not their number. அண்ணல் அறைந்த அறிவு may be the Lord's teaching or the knowledge of the Lord.

reading: Standing while rain and summer and long dew pass, while even the lake wanes, he spoke Sanskrit and Tamil together and showed grace to the lady.
nuance: காரிகையார் (the lady) is traditionally the Goddess, to whom Siva is said to have taught the Agamas. The first two lines may describe his standing through the seasons, or her long penance before he taught her. ஆரியம் here means Sanskrit, and the verse names it and Tamil as given together.

reading: How the soul is loosed, how it is bound, and how life departs in the blink of an eye: the Tamil word and the northern word, these two, teach him, and through them one can come to know him.
nuance: அவிழ்கின்ற, கட்டும் (loosing, binding) are read as release and bondage; the verse does not name the soul. The plain claim is that Tamil and Sanskrit equally lead to knowing the Lord.

title: குரு பாரம்பரியம்
theme: The line of gurus (குரு பாரம்பரியம்): Tirumular names the masters who received Nandi's grace, himself among eight, and the seven disciples who carry his mantra on; everything he has, he says, came by Nandi's grace, and the Lord charged the four Nandis with keeping the observances.
structure_note: The eight who received Nandi's grace (67), Tirumular's debt to Nandi (68), his seven disciples (69), and the four Nandis made masters and given their charge (70 to 72).

reading: If you seek the masters who received Nandi's grace: the four Nandis, the great sage Sivayoga, Patanjali and Vyaghra who worshipped at the hall, these with me make eight.
nuance: மன்று is the hall where Siva dances, by tradition Chidambaram, where Patanjali and Vyaghrapada are said to have seen the dance. The count is four plus three plus Tirumular himself.

reading: By Nandi's grace we gained the name of master; by Nandi's grace we sought out Mulan; what can Nandi's grace not do? With Nandi showing the way, I stayed in this land.
nuance: மூலனை நாடினோம் is traditionally taken of the body of Mulan the cowherd, which the sage entered and lived in; it may also mean seeking the root (மூலம்). The verse itself does not tell the story.

reading: Those who received the mantra in due succession, Malangan, Indran, Soman, Brahman, Rudran, Kalangi with Kanduru before his name, and Kanjamalaiyan, these seven are of my line.
nuance: Malangan and Indran are addressed later in the preface (75, 77). To make seven, கந்துரு is taken as a qualifier of காலாங்கி rather than a separate name; it could be read as an eighth name, and its sense is unclear.

reading: The four masters, one for each of the four directions, the four who took up many kinds of meaning, the four told 'may you gain all that I gained', the four became gods and became masters.
nuance: The four are probably the four Nandis of 67. Who says 'may you gain all that I gained' is not stated: Nandi, the Lord, or Tirumular. The phrase recalls 85, where Tirumular wishes his bliss on the whole world.

reading: What the Lord told the three and the four is a greatness beyond death and birth; the god who is the light of the three bright flames did not show that surpassing greatness.
nuance: The three and the four are not named. The three flames are traditionally sun, moon and fire. காட்டகிலானே may mean 'could not show' or 'did not show', and so the second half may mean the greatness lies beyond showing. The verse is obscure.

reading: 'Even if the flood rises and pours, keep the cool rich observances in all eight directions': so saying, the Lord with cool matted hair like tender coral gave grace to the four who were sunk deep in him.
nuance: நியமங்கள் are observances, one of the limbs of yoga in Tirumular's later tantras. எழுந்துநீர் பெய்யினும் may mean 'even if a flood comes' or 'rising, pour water' (an ablution). அழுந்திய (steeped, sunk in) describes the four's devotion.

title: திருமூலர் வரலாறு
theme: Tirumular's own story (திருமூலர் வரலாறு): with Nandi's feet on his head he came from Kailasa, saw the dance, served the Goddess, and stayed at Avaduthurai beneath the bodhi tree for ages, in this body. The Lord made him to sing the Lord in Tamil, and he wishes the bliss he gained on the whole world.
structure_note: His resolve to tell the Agama (73, 74); the reasons for his stay, told to Indra and Malangan (75 to 79); his long dwelling and the Lord's purpose in making him (80 to 87); then a run of verses on what Nandi gave him and what he has expounded (88 to 94). Verses 90 and 91 are linked by repeating விளக்கி.
source_issues: 76: lines 2 to 4 turn on Sanskrit forms (மிதாசனி, இதாசனி, உதாசனி) that do not yield a firm sense; the text may be corrupt.
83: சித்தசன் is unclear (a siddha, a proper name, or Manmatha).

reading: Placing Nandi's holy feet on my head, setting them within my mind and praising, thinking daily on the feet of Hara who wears the evening moon, I set out to tell the Agama.
nuance: போற்றிசெய் தந்தி is read போற்றிசெய்து அந்தி: the moon of evening. The verse sets the guru's feet before the Lord's, as the preface does throughout.

reading: Gaining the feet of gracious Nandi, who grants the teaching that bears the name Siva Agama, and after seeing the matchless dance in the flawless hall, I remained for seven crore ages without equal.
nuance: Line 1 may mean that the poet's work gained the name Siva Agama, or that he gained the Agama so named. எழுகோடி யுகம் is a figure of immense time. ஒப்பிலா may go with the ages or with himself.

reading: Hear the reason I stayed, Indra: having served the lady of rare austerity, rich in fortune, Bhuvanapati, I came with her out of love and devotion.
nuance: Indra is the disciple named in 69. புவனாபதி (lady of the worlds) and அருந்தவச் செல்வி are taken as the Goddess. Whether he came with her or came because of her is not clear.

reading: Through Sadasiva, the tattvas, the threefold Tamil and the Veda, I stayed till now keeping a measured diet, and with mind withdrawn and not indifferent, I came to know.
nuance: The verse rhymes on Sanskrit forms: மிதாசனி (one who eats sparingly), இதாசனி and உதாசனி (indifferent), which do not yield a firm sense. முத்தமிழ் is Tamil of letters, music and drama. The reading is a guess at the shape of the verse.

reading: Malangan, the reason I came here is to tell the Veda of noble limbs of the holy dance, spoken as root and limb with the fine-jewelled one of dark-blue body.
nuance: Malangan is the disciple named in 69. மூலாங்கம் and சீலாங்கம் are coined compounds; மூல may pun on Mulan. The 'Veda' he has come to tell is probably his own book.

reading: The fine-jewelled one is she whose name is unsurpassed bliss, who cut off my birth and took me as her own; she of glory is at Siva's Avaduthurai, and I reached her feet and stayed.
nuance: ஆவடுதண்டுறை is Tiruvavaduturai, where tradition places Tirumular. Here the Goddess, not Nandi or Siva, is the one who ends his births.

reading: I stayed joined to the one whose half is Siva's woman; I stayed at Siva's Avaduthurai; I stayed in the shade of Siva's bodhi tree; I stayed reciting Siva's names.
nuance: சிவபோதி (Siva's bodhi tree) and நற்போதி in 82 use the word for the Buddha's tree, here for the sacred fig under which the sage sat.

reading: I stayed in this body for countless crores; I stayed in the place where there is no night and day; I stayed at the feet the gods praise; I stayed beneath the twin feet of my Nandi.
nuance: இராப்பகல் அற்ற இடம் is traditionally a yogic state beyond the alternation of the breaths (read as sun and moon, day and night); plainly it is a place outside time. Staying in this body (இக்காயத்தே) for ages is offered as attainment, not as bondage.

reading: Why be born again later? People do not strive at austerity well beforehand. The Lord made me well so that I would render him well in Tamil.
nuance: தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறு is usually taken as 'to sing him well in Tamil'. The verse sets others' neglect of tapas against his own purpose. Sengalvaraya notes a parallel in Kandar Anubhuti 17, where the poet's learning is likewise the Lord's gift.

reading: Entering the city of Nandi, consort of the lady of wisdom, I too stayed for nine flawless crore ages beneath the good bodhi tree, worshipping the Lord and bathing him in the milk of wisdom.
nuance: ஞானப்பாலாட்டி may be 'bathing in the milk of wisdom' or a title of the Goddess (the nurse who gives wisdom's milk). The ages differ from 74's seven crore, which suggests figures of vastness.

reading: A Siva-sage who knows the way to go, a siddha, eminent among sages in conquering wisdom, came by the sky-path that bends toward the many gods, asuras and humans.
nuance: சித்தசன் is unclear: a siddha, a name, or Manmatha (சித்தஜன், born of mind) are all possible. Tradition reads the verse of Tirumular's own coming south from Kailasa through the sky.

reading: Among the books that excel in the mind, the Father here gave me by grace a body fitting the Veda recited as highest, and the origin that stands within.
nuance: ஒத்த உடலையும் (a fitting body too) and உள்நின்ற உற்பத்தி (the origin within) are hard to construe. The plain sense is that the body was given by grace, for the teaching; that fits Tirumular's high view of the body.

reading: May this world gain the bliss I gained: if one speaks the hidden meaning that holds the sky, the mantra felt within, that holds to the flesh, comes forward as one holds to it more and more.
nuance: The first line is the most quoted in the book and is plain. The rest is not: ஊன்பற்றி நின்ற உணர்வுறு மந்திரம் is traditionally the mantra present in the body as breath or as consciousness, and தலைப்படும் may mean it is attained or that it rises up.

reading: The gods go and fold their hands to the unborn Lord, great Nandi; never forgetting him, they can recite the garland of mantras in their hearts, joined to it firmly.
nuance: மந்திர மாலை (garland of mantras) is often taken as the Tirumanthiram itself. பிறப்பிலி (the unborn) is a title of Siva given here to Nandi.

reading: He set fire within its bounds and set the body, set the seven worlds so they keep within bounds, set the Tamil treatise so it keeps within bounds, and set meaning itself so it does not overflow.
nuance: The refrain is மிகாமை (not exceeding) after வைத்தான் (he set). The Lord's ordering of fire, body and worlds is extended to the Tamil sastra and its meaning. எங்குமி and தங்குமி may also divide as இகாமை (not leaving).

reading: Brahma and Vishnu, seeking his foot and crown, did not see his form; meeting again on earth, Achyuta said 'I did not see the foot', and Brahma lied, 'I saw the crown'.
nuance: The story of Siva as the endless column of fire. Vishnu admits failure and Brahma lies; the verse contrasts their honesty without stating a moral.

reading: Our Nandi, the Supreme never parted from bull, deer and axe, gave me release from the moving and unmoving world that is his imagining, and set his good feet on my head.
nuance: அற்றம் may be 'end', 'release' or 'secret'. கற்பனை ஆகும் சராசரம் (the world that is his imagining) can be read as the world being his creation or as its being illusory; the verse does not settle which.

reading: I have explained in full the known, knowledge and the knower, maya, the supreme power that comes from Mahamaya, the whole assembly, Siva himself, and the seed beyond the senses.
nuance: நேயம், ஞானம், ஞாதுரு are the triad of knowable, knowledge and knower. ஆயம் (group, assembly) and அகோசர வீயம் (the imperceptible seed) are technical and unclear. The verse claims the whole Siddhanta scheme for his book.

reading: Explaining, I came by the way of boundless Kailasa at the word of the unwavering dancer of bliss, Nandi of bliss and measureless greatness, the light of true wisdom that is the Supreme.
nuance: விளக்கி takes up 90's last word. The verse places his coming from Kailasa under the dancer's command, which is how tradition tells his journey south.

reading: By Nandi's grace I sought Mulan; then by Nandi's grace I became Sadasiva; by Nandi's grace I entered true wisdom; by Nandi's grace I stayed.
nuance: The four lines repeat நந்தி அருளாலே as 68 does. சதாசிவன் ஆயினேன் (I became Sadasiva) is a strong claim of identity with a form of Siva, attributed wholly to the guru's grace.

reading: If one stays, countless crores stay there within the consuming root; as sun and moon blaze with fierce fire, the melted hair shines with light.
nuance: மூலம் is traditionally the root centre of yoga, and அருக்கன், சோமன் (sun and moon) the two breath channels whose fire is raised. உருக்கிய ரோமம் (melted hair) is obscure; it may describe the yogi's body made radiant. இருக்கு may also pun on the Rig Veda. Both a plain and a yogic reading are uncertain here.

reading: Always I babble of great Nandi; I hold him in my heart night and day; I strive toward my Lord of soaring light, who is the Lord, a light shining by its own nature.
nuance: பிதற்றுகின்றேன் (I babble) is devotional self-belittling, preparing the chapter on modesty that follows. The last line runs Nandi and the Lord together.

title: அவையடக்கம்
theme: The poet's modesty before the assembly (அவையடக்கம்): no one knows the Lord's greatness or the root of the nameless flame, and Tirumular disclaims the skill of those who sing, dance and seek; yet the Lord can be known by those who contemplate him, though even sages and gods may miss the fruit of the knowledge of tattvas.

reading: Who knows the greatness of our Lord? Who knows his breadth and length? I tell of my not knowing the root of the one great nameless flame.
nuance: பேரறியாத may mean 'nameless' or 'whose name is unknown'. The great flame (பெருஞ்சுடர்) whose root is unknown recalls the fire column of 88. Sengalvaraya lists Tevaram parallels asking who knows his nature.

reading: I do not know how to sing in the way of those who can sing, nor dance in the way of those who can dance, nor seek in the way of those who can seek, nor search in the way of those who can search.
nuance: The four skills may be the forms of devotion (song and dance) and of inquiry (seeking and searching). The disclaimer is conventional in a preface, but here it covers both worship and knowledge.

reading: Those who honour him with abiding words of truth, even Brahma who afterward made the world, can come to know the Lord who rises within sweet music by contemplating him.
nuance: The syntax is loose: Brahma may be one of those who know him, or a contrast (even the creator must contemplate). உன்னும் (contemplating) is the verse's way to knowledge, against 95's 'who knows?'.

reading: The knowledge of the tattvas was told at the foot of the mountain; the sages and gods who waited there for release, staying apart and praising, do not know this fruit through devotion alone.
nuance: தாழ்வரை (foothill, slope) may be the place where the teaching was given, perhaps Kailasa. The last line is the hard part: பத்திமையால் இப்பயன் அறியாரே may mean they do not know the fruit by devotion, or that because of their devotion they do not know it (they praise rather than understand). Either way it seems to rank knowledge of tattvas above praise alone.

title: திருமந்திரத் தொகைச் சிறப்பு
theme: The greatness of the book's number (திருமந்திரத் தொகைச் சிறப்பு): Mulan's three thousand Tamil verses are Nandi's grace given for the world to know, and those who recite them each morning with understanding reach the Lord.
source_issues: 100: line 3 (புத்திசெய் பூர்வத்து மூவா யிரம்பொது) is obscure and may be corrupt.

reading: That the world should know the three thousand Tamil verses Mulan spoke is Nandi's grace; those who rise in the morning and recite them knowing their meaning will reach the Lord of the world.
nuance: கருத்தறிந்து (knowing the meaning) is the condition: recitation alone is not promised the fruit, as 64 says of the Agamas. The verse speaks of Mulan in the third person.

reading: As arranged, among the many kinds of good books, this is the end that is release, within the three thousand; the three thousand, set out for those who apply their minds, are common to all and give the distinction placed in them.
nuance: புத்திசெய் பூர்வத்து and மூவாயிரம் பொது are obscure. முத்தி முடிவு may mean that the book's goal is release or that it is the culmination of the teaching on release. The claim that the book is common (பொது) to all is a possible reading, not a sure one.

title: குரு மட வரலாறு
theme: The history of the guru mathas (குரு மட வரலாறு): seven lines of teaching descend in the true path down to Mulan's own, and he spoke the Agama in nine tantras and three thousand verses; the second verse names founders of the lines.
source_issues: 102: line 4 (நிலந்திகழ் மூவர் நிராமயத் தோரே) is unclear; the count of names does not obviously match seven mathas.

reading: Of the seven mathas that came down in the abiding true path, up to Mulan's matha that arises first, he spoke the beautiful Agama in nine tantras, three thousand verses, as their support.
nuance: சன்மார்க்கம் (the true path) in Siddhanta is the path of knowledge. முந்தி உதிக்கின்ற (arising first) may mean Mulan's matha is the earliest or the foremost. The verse speaks of Mulan in the third person; the count of nine tantras and three thousand verses is the book's own.

reading: From Kalangar, who mingles in grace, came Aghorar, Maligai Devar who gives good, Nathantar, Paramanandar of keen insight and Bhoga Devar; the three who shine on earth are of Niramaya.
nuance: The verse lists founders or teachers of the mathas. Kalangar is likely the Kalangi of 69. மூவர் (the three) and நிராமயத்தோர் (those of Niramaya, or 'the flawless ones') are unclear, so the number and grouping of the names is not certain.

title: திரு மும்மூர்த்திகளின் முறைமை
theme: The order of the three gods (மும்மூர்த்திகளின் முறைமை): Siva is the one source, and Brahma and Vishnu are his aspects or parts, holding their place from him; those who split the three into rival gods and quarrel over them have not understood.
structure_note: Polemic verses against dividing the three (104, 107, 110) alternate with verses on how the one Lord takes on the three functions and forms (105, 106, 111, 112); 108 is Tirumular's own commission, 109 puts Siva's grace above every other god.
source_issues: 105: இருவினைககு is a misprint for இருவினைக்கு, and உலகல் is probably உலகில்.
107: நமககு is a misprint for நமக்கு; வயனம் is obscure and may be corrupt.

reading: For one who understands the measureless youth, end and limit, measured time and the four, Sankara is unwearied, and the measureless greatness his devotees speak of is what reaches Hari and Brahma.
nuance: The verse is compressed and its first two lines are obscure: நாலும் (the four) is unexplained, and அளவில் may mean 'measureless' or 'in measure'. The last line is commonly taken to mean that Hari and Brahma hold their greatness from Siva, which fits the chapter, but the syntax does not settle it.

reading: The first Lord, the one coloured like a fine jewel and the one on the petals of the first lotus are, on examination, one in their continuity; those who do not say so divide them and quarrel throughout the world.
nuance: ஆதிப் பிரான் is Siva, அணிமணி வண்ணன் Vishnu and the one on the lotus Brahma. தொடர்ச்சியில் ஒன்று (one in continuity) does not say the three are identical; it may mean they form one sequence or one lineage from a single source. பேதித்து பிணங்குதல names sectarian quarrelling.

reading: The Lord stands beyond the two kinds of deeds; the seed became the great god for the world; those who say the Lord is this or that have no understanding, while those who held fast knew the root.
nuance: இருவினை is good and bad deeds. பீசம் (bija, seed) is unclear: the Lord as seed of the world, or a seed-syllable. தூசு பிடித்தவர் (those who held the cloth) is taken as those who clung to the Lord as a child holds a garment's hem; தூர் (root, base) may be the Lord as source.

reading: With Siva first, the three and the five excel; from them come twelve, one joined with one; from them bindu and nada rise; and Sankara, first in the assembly, has these as his own name.
nuance: The numbers (three, five, twelve, one with one) are not explained in the verse. Tradition reads them as groups of deities or powers emanating from Siva, but which groups is not fixed by the text. The plain point is that every emanation, up to bindu and nada, is Siva's own name and form.

reading: Reckoning by that way, knowing the fruit, Brahma and Vishnu are not strangers to us; they are kin of three-eyed Nandi, and you will gain blessing through those gods.
nuance: வயனம் is obscure; it may stand for வசனம் (word) or a blessing. தமர் (one's own people) makes Brahma and Vishnu Siva's kin and so worthy of regard, not rivals. The verse accepts their worship within Siva's order.

reading: As I bowed and worshipped the milk-white one surrounded by his court of deathless gods, he said: 'You are equal to Mal and to Brahma; give our feet to the world.'
nuance: The speaker is taken to be Tirumular, and the verse as Siva's commission to him to teach. Who is 'equal to Mal and Brahma' is not wholly clear: it may be Tirumular, honoured as a teacher, or the phrase may compare Siva's gift. நம் அடி நல்கிடு, 'give our feet', makes the teaching the giving of Siva's feet.

reading: Whether gods or humans, there is no separate god to settle on and think of other than the grace of Siva of the honeyed konrai; it is that grace which knows those who dwell in flesh.
nuance: The verse puts grace (அருள்) in the place of a god: the only deity is Siva's grace. The last line can also be read as 'it is that which those in the body must come to know'.

reading: The ignorant do not know that the great light, examined, stood as three and as five in the beginning; they babble, dividing it into the Lord, tall Mal and Brahma by their functions.
nuance: மூன்று ஐந்து may be the three gods and the five (adding Maheswara and Sadasiva), or the five acts of the Lord. நீதிக்கண் is read here as 'by their offices'. ஆதர் means the blind or the ignorant; பிதற்றுதல் is a strong word for babbling.

reading: One in the supreme, inside and outside, becoming Vishnu and Brahma in their boons, taking many natures in their ranks, he stands concealed and works dissolution.
nuance: The verse gives the one Lord the three functions: preserving as Vishnu, creating as Brahma, dissolving himself. கரத்தினுள் is taken as 'in concealment' (from கர, hide); 'in the hand' is also possible. வரம் and தரம் (boon, rank) are uncertain.

reading: One part of him is Sadasiva our Lord; one part joins and stays in the sky; one part as lord stands in the body and gives it breath; and one part is the one of the waters.
nuance: சலமயன் (the one of water) is unclear: Vishnu lying on the waters, or Siva bearing the Ganga. The third line is the most important for the book as a whole: the Lord is the one who breathes in every body.

title: உபதேசம்
theme: Teaching (உபதேசம்): the Lord comes down as the guru and burns away the soul's impurity, which is beginningless like the soul; through grace and Siva-yoga the freed come to rest in Sivam, in a state of stillness, 'sleep' and silence that cannot be told. The means offered are the guru's form, name and word and Nandi's feet.
structure_note: The verses form an andhadi: each opens with the word that ends the one before (களிம்பறுத்தானே, களிம்பறுத்தான்; பதியே, பதி; and so on). The movement is from the guru's descent and the removal of malas (113 to 120), through Siva-yoga and the siddhas (121 to 129), the dance and the gain of those who worship it (130 to 132), images of union (133 to 137), to the feet, the guru and Nandi as refuge (138 to 142).
source_issues: 125: line 2 reads முள்கொண்டோ ர் with a stray space, for முள்கொண்டோர்.
121: வியாக்கிரத்தே (literally 'in the tiger') is obscure and may be a corruption of ஜாக்கிரத்தே (in the waking state).
133: இருமையுங் கேட்டு may be a misreading of இருமையுங் கெட்டு ('with duality destroyed'), which would change the sense.
120 (ஆமேவு) and 135 (ஆண்டுகொள் அப்பிலே) are obscure and may be corrupt.

reading: Coming down from the sky, taking a body to answer my deeds, setting his cool feet on my head as a guard, melting me from within and showing me in the eye an incomparable bliss, he cut away the verdigris.
nuance: களிம்பு is the green tarnish on copper; tradition takes it as the soul's root impurity (ஆணவம்), and the verse as the Lord descending as guru. வினைக்கு ஈடாய் may mean the body he took suits the disciple's deeds, so that the Lord meets the soul in a form it can receive.

reading: He cut away the verdigris, our Nandi with the eye in his forehead; cutting it, he opened the eye of grace, showed a radiant light that tarnish cannot touch, and set coral in crystal: he is the Lord.
nuance: பளிங்கில் பவளம் பதித்தான் (set coral in crystal) is symbolic: commonly read as the red Lord shining in the soul once it is clear like crystal. பதி, the verse's last word, is both 'Lord' and the first word of the next verse.

reading: Of the three named Pati, Pasu and Pasam, Pasu and Pasam are beginningless like Pati; Pasu and Pasam cannot go and reach Pati, but when Pati draws near, Pasu and Pasam do not remain.
nuance: The verse states the Saiva Siddhanta triad of Lord, soul and bond, and makes all three without beginning. The last line is traditionally read as the end of the soul's bondage (its being a பசு, a bound creature), not of the soul itself; the verse alone does not make that distinction. Approach is one-way: the soul cannot reach the Lord, the Lord must come.

reading: Like fire that rises from bamboo, Nandi, the king who has made his home in the temple called this body, removes the three malas more tenderly than a mother and rises as a sun that is the water of compassion.
nuance: Fire latent in bamboo, which comes out by friction, is the Lord hidden in the body. The body is called a temple (மெய் எனும் கோயில்), not a filthy frame. The last line mixes images: a sun that is the water (தோயம்) of mercy; tradition takes it as grace that both burns impurity and cools.

reading: As a sunstone does not burn the cotton around it until it stands in the sun's presence, and then burns it, so the malas end before the sun appears.
nuance: The sunstone is commonly taken as the soul, the cotton as the malas and the sun as the Lord or the guru. The point is that the soul has the power to burn its impurity only in the Lord's presence.

reading: Making known that the malas are five, he removed them in grace; Nandi in that common hall, who is Sadasiva of the five stations, cleared away the five domains and, knowing them, desired the good within.
nuance: Five malas are traditionally ஆணவம், கன்மம், மாயை, மாயேயம் and திரோதாயி, though the verse does not name them. தலங்கள் ஐந்து (five stations) and புலங்கள் (domains, senses) are unclear, and the last line is obscure.

reading: When awareness, hanging on the five senses, was lost like water sunk in depths with no outlet, and was as if it had perished within awareness, the supreme guru makes known the sign.
nuance: நான்றது (hung on, depended on) and நீர் ஆழம் (deep water) are the key images. அறிவு அறிவுள்ளே அழிந்தது is hard: perhaps the soul's knowing swallowed by the senses, or a positive merging. குறி (sign, mark) is left unexplained.

reading: Like the swan that parts milk from water, he alone, eternally, in the solitary hall, makes what is lodged in the many fiery faculties into seeds that have touched the fire and will not sprout into the seven births.
nuance: A roasted seed does not sprout: deeds burnt by grace no longer yield births. Who parts milk from water is not stated; it may be the Lord, the guru or the discerning soul. ஆமேவு, the opening, is obscure.

reading: Having destroyed the seed, with the pure turiya state arising strongly in waking, bonds cut, senses and life become one, they remain with the body as if dead: these are the Siva-yogis.
nuance: வியாக்கிரம் (literally tiger) is obscure; it is often taken as ஜாக்கிரம், the waking state, giving turiya in waking. 'Dead with the body' is taken as dead to the senses while alive. Sengalvaraya notes a parallel in Kandar Alangaram 19.

reading: Siva-yoga is to know the conscient and the non-conscient, enter the yoga of tapas, become one's own light, not take to false yoga, and go to his abode; Nandi of the nava-yoga gave it to us.
nuance: சித்து, அசித்து are the conscient (souls) and the non-conscient (matter). அவயோகம் is read as wrong or lower yoga. நவயோகம் may mean 'the new yoga' or 'nine yogas'; the text doesn't decide.

reading: He gave the truth that he is himself the whole world; he gave the world the gods do not know; he gave the holy feet that dance in the sacred hall; he gave the open space of grace in great bliss.
nuance: The anaphora on அளித்தான் (he gave) builds a list of gifts that rise from knowledge to bliss. Sengalvaraya notes a parallel in Tirumurugatruppadai 293.

reading: Those who see clearly how space went into space and mingled, how sweetness went into sweetness and subsided, how light went into light and was absorbed: they are the Siva-siddhas.
nuance: அளி can be honey, the bee or grace; whichever, the pattern is like merging into like. Three images of union without remainder.

reading: Siddhas are those who have seen Sivaloka here, who hold within them sound and sound's end; eternal, stainless, free of affliction, the far-supreme freed ones, their release begins from the thirty-six.
nuance: சத்தமும் சத்த முடிவும் are taken as nada and nadanta. முப்பத்தாறு is the thirty-six tattvas. 'Sivaloka here' (இங்கே) makes release something seen in this life.

reading: Taking the thirty-six as the rungs of a ladder to release, entering the inner light of incomparable bliss, seeing the unspeakable Sivam and becoming clear, they remained settled in that state.
nuance: The tattvas, which elsewhere unfold the world downward from Siva, are here climbed upward as rungs. Sengalvaraya notes parallels in Kandar Anubhuti 47 and Kandar Alangaram 55.

reading: They remained having become Sivam and everything; they remained watching all of Siva's acts; they remained knowing the nature of the three times; they remained in the idleness that came when the loss had come.
nuance: சோம்பு (idleness) is turned to praise: the stillness of one who has nothing left to do. இழவு (loss) is not said: loss of self, of the world, or of striving.

reading: The idle ones dwell in pure space, lie in pure space; their awareness is where the Veda ends, and what they saw is sleep within that Veda.
nuance: The Kural lists sloth and sleep among the marks of those headed for ruin (605); Tirumular makes the same words name the freed. சுருதி முடிந்திடம் (where the Veda ends) is Vedanta, and சுருதிக்கண் தூக்கம் rest in it. The inversion is deliberate, but it is about stillness in Sivam, not worldly work.

reading: Sleeping, they saw Sivaloka within themselves; sleeping, Siva-yoga within themselves; sleeping, Siva-bhoga within themselves; how could that state be told?
nuance: The world, the union and the enjoyment of Siva are all found inside (தம்முள்ளே). The sleep is a sleep with awareness; Sengalvaraya notes Tiruppugazh 757, 'those who sleep with awareness'.

reading: However far one's knowing reaches, so far the first Hara gives grace; he who dances in the matchless hall for Uma to see is a ruby redder than the red sky, a rich flame.
nuance: The first line makes grace proportioned to the seeker's capacity. The red sky and ruby fix Siva's colour as red, as in 114.

reading: Within the ruby an emerald light, within the ruby an emerald mansion: what a gain did they gain who cherished and worshipped the holy dance in the hall of finest gold!
nuance: Ruby and emerald are traditionally Siva and Uma, the green one within the red. ஆணிப்பொன் is gold of the finest touch. The last line's question is answered in 132.

reading: They gained in this world the great path that does not part from him, the great fruit of not being born, the great attainment that does not part from that hall, and the greatness of not speaking with the world.
nuance: உலகுடன் பேசாப் பெருமை may be silence, or freedom from worldly converse and ties. All four gains are had 'in the world' (உலகில்).

reading: Who but our Lord knows greatness and smallness, and knows the hard and the easy? Those who, in one birth (or in one-pointedness), drew the five within like a tortoise and heard both, remained without flaw.
nuance: The third line nearly repeats Kural 126 (ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), where ஒருமை is usually taken as 'one birth'; here it may keep that sense or mean one-pointedness. இருமையும் கேட்டு is unclear: 'heard both' (this world and the next, or both teachings), or, if கேட்டு is a misreading of கெட்டு, 'with duality destroyed'.

reading: Like ghee mixed in pure milk, those who feel beyond words what the noble teacher of waveless mind speaks, once their body falls here, become the reality mixed in the shoreless light.
nuance: ஆரியன் here is the noble teacher. Ghee in milk is present throughout yet unseen until churned; it may be the Lord in the soul or the teaching in the hearer. சத்து (being, reality) is what the knower becomes.

reading: If the five beginning with sound settle back by their own path, where else is there for the conscient to join except the Conscient? In pure space flame joins flame; grasp this meaning and be ruled, as in water.
nuance: சித்துக்குச் சித்து: the conscient soul's only home is the conscient Lord. ஆண்டுகொள் அப்பிலே is obscure; அப்பு (water) leads into the salt image of 136.

reading: As salt, named and given form by the sun's heat on the water's sharpness, becomes one again in the water it meets, so, it is said, the soul subsides into Sivam.
nuance: The salt was always of the water and returns to it. The image suggests non-difference; Siddhanta tradition reads it as union in which the soul does not perish, which the verse alone does not settle. அடங்கும் (subsides, is contained) is milder than 'is lost'.

reading: In the great universe that subsides, the atom-worlds go and find no room; is there anything other than this? If you see the shore of the life that stands in each body, it is the holy feet of the one who stood firm.
nuance: கடம் (pot) stands for the body. The first two lines are obscure; the plain sense of the last two is that the limit of every soul is the Lord's feet.

reading: Examine it and the holy feet are Sivam; think on it and the holy feet are Sivaloka; speak of it and the holy feet are the path to travel; the holy feet are refuge for those clear within.
nuance: The feet are at once the Lord, his world and the way there. தஞ்சம் is refuge. The 'clear within' (உள் தெளிவார்) leads into 139, which defines clarity.

reading: Clarity is seeing the guru's holy form, uttering the guru's holy name, hearing the guru's holy words and thinking on the guru's form.
nuance: The four acts engage eye, tongue, ear and mind. Clarity (தெளிவு) is not reached by argument here but by devotion to the guru.

reading: Of themselves the five senses come under one's control; of themselves they go into his control; of themselves they turn their channels inward, once one has met our Lord alone.
nuance: தன்வசம் can mean 'in one's own power' or 'in his (the Lord's) power', and the first two lines may differ on just that. மடைமாறும் (the sluice turns) is an irrigation image: the senses' flow is redirected. The key word is தானே: the control is not achieved by effort but follows from meeting the Lord.

reading: What one meets is Nandi's pair of holy feet; what one thinks on is Nandi's red holy form; what one praises in truth is Nandi's name; what stands within the mind is Nandi's golden feet.
nuance: சந்திப்பது picks up the last word of 140. Nandi is both Siva and the guru-lineage; the verse leaves them as one.

reading: Those who placed our meritorious Nandi, who gives understanding, within their understanding became meritorious; with their eyes overflowing at the Lord's dance and the Veda praising, they went and reached the sky.
nuance: போதம் (understanding) is played on: Nandi gives it, and is placed in it. விண் may be heaven or the space of Sivam the earlier verses speak of.

title: யாக்கை நிலையாமை
theme: The impermanence of the body (யாக்கை நிலையாமை): the body is a clay pot, a thatched hut, a walled temple that falls apart; when the life that dwelt in it leaves, kin weep, burn it, bathe and forget, and only vows and knowledge go with the dead.
structure_note: Two kinds of verse alternate: scenes of a death and its funeral (145, 147, 148, 150, 151, 153, 155, 157, 162), and images of the body as a made thing, pot or hut or temple, often in riddling numbers (143, 146, 154, 158, 159, 161). 165 and 166 turn to what follows death, and 167 closes on the dancer who has left the skin bag.
source_issues: 163 line 1 reads முந்_று, apparently a damaged முந்நூறு (three hundred); line 3 reads பன்னிரண்டி ஆண்டினில், probably for பன்னிரண்டாண்டினில்.
155 line 4 (மதுவூர வாங்கியே), 156 lines 3 and 4, 157 line 3 (வேர்த்தலை போக்கி) and 161 line 3 (ஊடு வரியாமை) are obscure and may be corrupt.
167 shares most of its wording with Naladiyar 26; which text borrowed is not settled here.

reading: From one clay come two kinds of vessel, one that stays firm and one bound up with bad deeds; as the unfired returns to clay when rain falls from the sky, so people die past counting.
nuance: The two vessels are most simply the fired and the unfired pot; line 2 (திண்ணென்று இருந்தது தீவினைச் சேர்ந்தது) can also mean that what seemed firm was itself joined to bad deeds, so that no body is truly fired. எண்ணின்றி may be 'without number' or 'without their thinking of it'.

reading: When the roof that held one's goods falls, worn with use, the women and children who ate from it do not follow; nothing goes along the road with the dead but the vows they kept and the knowledge they gained.
nuance: The roof (கூரை) is the body, as in 146 and 161. விரதம் (vow, observance) and ஞானம் are the only companions named, not wealth or kin.

reading: The whole town gathers and wails aloud, takes away his name and calls him a corpse, carries him to the thorny burning ground and burns him, then bathes in water and stops thinking of him.
nuance: The name is removed before the body: பேரினை நீக்கிப் பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு. The last act is not the burning but the forgetting (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்) that the bath completes.

reading: There are two posts, one ridge beam and thirty-two great rafters in the frame; the roof above comes apart, and once it has, the life cannot enter it again as before.
nuance: The hut is the body: the two posts are the legs and the ridge beam is commonly taken as the spine. What the thirty-two rafters (பருங்கழி) stand for is not fixed; the ribs or the teeth are the usual guesses.

reading: Sickness ripened, the deeds that were done ran out, the body came apart and its frame rotted; they put a hand to the nose, covered him, carried him off and set out an offering for the crows.
nuance: சீக்கை and அலகு are unclear: சீக்கை is read as sickness or phlegm, அலகு as the beam of the frame. Death follows when the store of past deeds is used up (செய்வினை மூட்டிற்ற). The hand at the nose tests for breath; the crows' offering is the rice set out at the rites, or the body itself left to crows.

reading: He had food cooked and ate it, talked privately with his tender wife, said his left side ached a little, lay down, and lay there gone.
nuance: The verse is a row of ordinary verbs ending in கிடந்தொழிந்தாரே, so that the death arrives as one more act of the day. இறை here means 'a little', not 'the Lord'.

reading: In the public square the man raised a mansion, in the square he gained a palanquin and rode in it, in the square he gave away three crores; when the cry came that he had gone, he did not turn back.
nuance: மன்றத்தே repeats three times: a whole public life of building, honour and giving. The palanquin may be a mark of honour, or, as in 153, the bier he rides at last. சென்றத்தா என்ன is unclear; it may be the mourners' cry 'he has gone, father'.

reading: With sweet talk they marry and live with that husband till their love is sated and they stop thinking of him; then they lay him on the bier, weep as is fitting, burn the bond in fire and make the offering.
nuance: வாசந்தி in line 1 is obscure; it rhymes with ஆசந்தி (bier) in line 3, setting the wedding against the funeral. பாசம் may be the bond of love that is burned with him or simply the body. The verse makes the wife's mourning a matter of form (அமைய அழுதிட்டு).

reading: The physician lets go the hand after feeling the pulse, the mind fails and the axle breaks, and the five who ate rice with ghee poured on it are gone; while the kohl-eyed wife and the wealth stay behind, this is how one takes leave and quits the body.
nuance: The five (ஐவர்) are traditionally the five senses, fed well and the first to leave; the same five return in 188. அச்சற (the axle breaking) is read of the body as a cart. What stays (wife, wealth) and what goes (the man) are set side by side.

reading: The pandal has come apart, the storehouse has lost its fastenings, all nine gates are shut together; as the time of pain brings defilement on and on, the loving ones wept and went away.
nuance: The nine gates (ஒன்பது வாசல்) are the body's nine openings, an image Tirumular uses again in 175. துரிசு (defilement, fault) may be the decay of the corpse.

reading: The lord of the land, the chief of our town, mounts for the last time a palanquin of the burning ground; with the people following behind and drums beating in front, this is how the land's lord walks.
nuance: Every mark of a royal procession is kept, the palanquin, the following crowd, the drums, but the palanquin is the bier (காட்டுச் சிவிகை). The verse lets the irony stand without comment.

reading: Thirty and thirty and thirty-six live in a temple with a well-built wall; once that walled temple fell to ruin, all of them alike ran off.
nuance: 30 + 30 + 36 makes ninety-six, the number of the body's constituents (tattvas) in a later Tamil count; that is how the verse is traditionally read, though it names no tattvas. The body is called a கோயில (temple) here, an idea Tirumular develops elsewhere.

reading: Leaving behind the woman with honeyed hair, the wealth and the house, he mounts the platform, and looking toward the common burning ground outside the town they lifted him, set him down and went away.
nuance: இதணம் (a raised platform) is taken as the bier. மதுவூர வாங்கியே in line 4 is obscure; it echoes மதுவூர் in line 1 and may be corrupt.

reading: Even seeing him set down and left, people think the rare wealth they seek will not leave them; those who chase it like madness grow weak without ever leaving off.
nuance: The first line takes up வைத்தகன்றார் from 155. Lines 3 and 4 (பிச்சது வாய்ப்பின் தொடர்வுறு மற்றவர் எச்சகலா) are obscure, and this reading of them is a guess.

reading: The kin who rise up wailing, the wives and the children, turn back at the edge of the town; after that they strip him, pile the wood and light the fire, then plunge headfirst into the water, people without justice.
nuance: நீதியிலோர் (those without justice) is a harsh last word for the mourners; it may mean only that they do what custom requires and no more. வேர்த்தலை போக்கி is unclear.

reading: Over the whole wide land the potter shaped pots from the tank's clay; when a pot breaks people keep the pieces as shards, but when the body breaks they will not keep it even a moment.
nuance: The broken pot is still worth something, the broken body nothing. Line 1 (வளத்திடை முற்றத்தோர்) is hard to construe.

reading: Five tufts, six braids, thirty joints, eighteen supports, nine pandals and fifteen rows: it lay burnt, and we know nothing beyond that.
nuance: The numbers describe the body as a built thing, but what each stands for is not given and I can't fix it; tradition matches them to the elements, senses and other parts. The plain point is the last line: all this lay burnt, and what came after is unknown.

reading: They chopped fig fruit and good spinach seed, put them in the pot and cooked a gruel; when the spinach seed ate the fig, those who held the knife went to the burning ground.
nuance: A riddle with no key in the verse. The fig and the seed are commonly taken as parts of the body, or as body and karma, and the gruel as the body's making; I can't fix the reference. Only the end, the cooks going to the burning ground, is plain.

reading: There is no ridge above and no eave below; there are two posts and one ridge beam; it is a silver dwelling thatched not by those who thatch with palm leaf but by a craftsman.
nuance: The two posts and one beam repeat 146. வேலையான் may be the craftsman who made the body, taken as the Lord, and வெள்ளித் தளிகை (silver dish or dwelling) is unclear. Line 3 (ஊடு வரியாமை) is hard to construe.

reading: The hall lies there but its adornments are gone; the dancing rhythm has ceased altogether; some sing and weep in tune, and they put it in the fire they gathered.
nuance: The hall (கூடம்) is the body; the ceased rhythm (இலயம்) may be breath or pulse. தீயவைத்தார் plays on தீ (fire) and தீய (the bad thing), so the corpse becomes something unclean to be burned.

reading: The egg was born in three hundred days, though nothing was put there, poor people; at twelve years it knew marriage, at seventy it perished, and you do not see the ruin.
nuance: The egg is the body, carried about three hundred days in the womb. இட்டது தானிலை ஏதேனும் is obscure: perhaps that no one can say who laid it. The verse compresses a whole life into three numbers.

reading: While the lamp bowl stays, he took away the flame; fools who don't know it is over cry aloud, and the world, not knowing that dawn turns to darkness, lies sunk and trembles.
nuance: The bowl is the body and the flame the life. The taker (கொண்டான்) is not named; Death or the Lord both fit. The mourners are called fools for weeping over the bowl.

reading: Those who do not worship the form of the one with spreading konrai blossoms, who made body and life, lie suffering in the seventh hell, where they cry out as their entrails burn.
nuance: The konrai wearer is Siva. மாயன் may be another epithet of him (the wondrous one) or name Vishnu as maker; and the line may mean not worshipping him who made body and life, or not worshipping him with body and life. ஏழா நரகு is read as the seventh, lowest hell.

reading: With umbrella, horse and victorious sword the time passed in between; when the man goes, at that moment the precious life reaches its place, left or right.
nuance: The umbrella, horse and sword are the signs of rule, the life between birth and death. இடம் வலம் (left, right) is commonly taken as the bad or good destination the life reaches according to its deeds; it may also mean only that it goes wherever it goes. Lines 2 and 3 are hard to construe.

reading: Once the dancer who stood in the skin bag, worked it to the end and fed it has left, what does it matter if crows carry off this nest, onlookers revile it, drops of milk are poured on it or many praise it?
nuance: The dancer (கூத்தன்) is the life that moved the body; a theological reading makes it the dancing Lord. பாற்றுளி (drops of milk) is the milk poured in the funeral rites, and பழிச்சில் means 'if they praise', answering பழிக்கில் (if they revile). The body is called கூடு, a nest or cage.

title: செல்வம் நிலையாமை
theme: The impermanence of wealth (செல்வம் நிலையாமை): wealth wanes like the moon, sinks like a capsizing boat and is taken by the stronger, as honey is taken from bees; the lasting wealth is the Lord, and one who gives up his wealth and thinks of him need not fear Death.
structure_note: Most verses set fleeting wealth against the Lord as true wealth (168, 169, 173, 176); 171 and 175 share a closing line about being shown up and abandoned, and 172 and 174 urge giving wealth away.
source_issues: 168 line 4 (மருளும் பினையவன்) and 176 lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe and may be corrupt.

reading: Before favour, king, elephants, chariots and wealth pass into others' hands, if with clear understanding, while life lasts, one joins the one who is true wealth, confusion ends; that is the great austerity.
nuance: செல்வன் (the wealthy one) is taken as the Lord, the wealth that is not lost. அருள் at the head of the list is odd among worldly goods; it may mean a patron's favour. Line 4 (மருளும் பினையவன்) is hard to construe.

reading: Wealth that bewilders is like the moving moon with its great waning, and needs no more said of it; seek the king of the gods without confusion, and he becomes great wealth, like a rain cloud.
nuance: The two images are paired: the moon that grows only to wane, and the rain cloud that pours. இரும்பிழப்பு is read as இரும் இழப்பு (great loss); வானவர் கோன் (king of the gods) is Siva here.

reading: Seeing that even their own shadow is no help to them, the foolish still sit saying 'this wealth is mine'; your life will go, though it was born together with the body; see the light the eye sees.
nuance: The shadow that cannot help its owner shows how little anything outside one is one's own. The last line (கண்ணது காணொளி) may mean simply 'see with your own eyes' or point to an inner light; both readings stand.

reading: Bees find the scent of flowers, gather the honey and its sweetness and store it on a branch; the strong drive them off and take it, and this is how what was gathered was shown up and abandoned.
nuance: The hoarder is the bee and the strong (வலியார்) are whoever takes the hoard: thieves, kings, heirs. The verse states the image and leaves the lesson to the reader.

reading: Be clear and settled, and once clear do not be troubled; do not churn about like a river in flood; turn your wealth away and get rid of it, and when Death comes you may even leap past him.
nuance: மாற்றிக் களைவீர் மறுத்து may mean giving the wealth away or renouncing it; either way the hold on it is broken. குதிக்கலும் ஆமே (one may even leap) echoes the old phrase for escaping Death; whether that means not dying, or meeting death unafraid and free, the verse doesn't say.

reading: The wealth and riches you delight in go like a boat on water that capsizes; people do not examine and see that a small casket has been set within the body that comes apart, as the means of release.
nuance: சிமிழ் (a small casket) is unexplained; it is traditionally taken as the place within the body where the Lord is found, such as the heart. The verse contrasts the boat that sinks with a treasure already inside.

reading: People say of their life, wife, children and brothers 'what limit is there to what is ours?'; to those who share out the bright wealth that comes to them, a helper who answers when called may come.
nuance: Line 2 (அளவு ஏது எமக்கு) may be boasting ('our wealth has no limit') or worry ('what is enough for us?'). கூவும் துணை (the helper who answers a call) may be the Lord or the merit of giving.

reading: Craving has grown great, and no one here holds to truth; there is one post to tie to and nine ways out; the mother and kin who set it up come and bow, and then, this is how they showed it up and abandoned it.
nuance: The post (தறி) is the body where the life is tethered, the nine ways its openings, as in 152. The last line repeats 171's, so the kin who raised the body leave it as the strong leave the bees' hive. Why the verse sits in a chapter on wealth is unclear unless the body is the first wealth.

reading: When the life leaves the body and runs, there is no way to fight it; think of the Lord, and Death's true messengers, who stand ready to release, will not even think of burning you.
nuance: அண்ணலை எண்ணும் can be a command ('think of the Lord') or describe those who do. The last two lines are hard to construe; the reading that Death's messengers spare the one who thinks of the Lord is the plainest but not certain.

title: இளமை நிலையாமை
theme: The impermanence of youth (இளமை நிலையாமை): the sun's daily course and the calf grown old show that youth is passing, yet people do not take it in; the time to think of Siva and praise him is now, while life and youth remain.
