structure_note: Verses on time's passing (177, 182, 184, 185) alternate with Tirumular's own voice: the aged man no longer desired (180) and the one who clings to the Lord's feet and saw him in his days (181, 186).
source_issues: 177 line 1 reads கிழக்கெழுந்த் தோடிய, with a stray pulli on த்; probably கிழக்கெழுந்தோடிய.
182 line 4 reads நினைப்பவர்ககு, a misprint for நினைப்பவர்க்கு.

reading: Even seeing the sun that rose in the east run its course and fall in the west, eyeless people do not grasp it; even seeing a young calf become an old bull in a few days and fall, people of the wide world do not grasp it.
nuance: The two lines are built alike (விழக்கண்டும் தேறார்): the day and a life follow the same arc. விழியிலா (without eyes) is the blindness of those who see and do not understand.

reading: Many years have gone by, and none have taken the Father to themselves, entered and known him; though the long ages give still longer time, they do not know the flame of the lamp whose wick is raised.
nuance: தூண்டு விளக்கு (a lamp whose wick is pushed up to burn bright) is traditionally taken as the inner light, or the Lord within. The point stands either way: more time does not bring knowing.

reading: Youth wears away and is gone at last, and after one's power for hard deeds is spent; so think on and hold to Nandi of the spreading locks into which the Ganga leapt, while life is still in you.
nuance: The verb அற்ற (ended) runs through the first three lines: youth ended, strength ended, the Ganga's rush ended in his hair. The last line makes the urgency plain: உயிருள்ள போதே.

reading: Before, tender women desired me as the juice pressed from crushed sugarcane; to those bejewelled women with breasts like buds, I who was like sugarcane am now like the bitter kaanjiram fruit too.
nuance: The poet speaks of himself: the same man was cane and is now strychnine fruit (காஞ்சிரங்காய்) to the same women. The உம் in காயுமொத்தேன் may mean he was both in turn.

reading: Seeing the times called child, youth and old man pass, people still do not understand; I lie at the feet of the one who passed beyond the world and cut through the cosmos, and desire them still more.
nuance: ஞாலம் கடந்து அண்டம் ஊடறுத்தான் (who passed the world and pierced the cosmos) fits the tradition of Siva as the boundless column of fire. The verse turns from what others fail to see to the poet's own clinging.

reading: For those who rise in the morning, day after day evening falls and the life span passes; though that Lord is hard to hold, he gives joy to those who think of him fittingly.
nuance: சலவியன் is obscure: perhaps 'the changeful one', 'the one hard to approach' or 'the one who moves'. ஏல நினைப்பவர் may be those who think of him fittingly or those who think of him early.

reading: Five thick needles live in one bag; the five needles are a flying beast; when frost falls on the five needles, the needle bag itself flies off.
nuance: A riddle. The bag is commonly read as the body and the five needles as the five senses; பனித்தலைப் பட்டால் (when frost falls on the head) may be old age and grey hair. The four lines all begin பருவூசி, which may also play on பருவம் (season of life).

reading: People do not understand at all that the moon and the burning sun stand within and measure out the world; those bound for heaven and those bound by deeds alike are cut down at the counted thirty.
nuance: கண்ணதும் is read as the moon, the other eye of the sky; yogic readings make sun and moon the two breaths. எண்ணுறும் முப்பதில் (at the counted thirty) may be the thirty days of a month or a span of years; I can't fix it.

reading: Seeing the sixteen kalas joined and standing together, the base do not reflect; after harsh Death has put them in the pit of the womb, they fall into it again, their bewilderment not ending.
nuance: The sixteen kalas (ஈரெண் கலை) are the moon's sixteen digits, full only for a moment before waning; in yoga they have an inner sense as well. கருக்குழி (the womb pit) names rebirth.

reading: In the days you have, that youth may not pass in vain, praise him in song in the days you have; not knowing in the days I had what would be cast off, I stayed in the days I had and saw.
nuance: எய்திய நாளில் (in the days one has reached) opens every line. எறிவது (what is thrown or cast) is unclear: the body, youth, or Death's blow. The object of கண்டேன் (I saw) is left unsaid, taken as the Lord.

title: உயிர் நிலையாமை
theme: The impermanence of life (உயிர் நிலையாமை): the life dwells in the body as a king in a drum or a lord over five guardians of a field, and leaves when its summons comes; so praise the Lord, do good, and share your food while there is time.
structure_note: Riddling images of the life in the body and its leaving (188, 189, 193, 194) alternate with direct urging (187, 195, 196); 190 and 191 fault those who do not know the Lord within or see time measured out.
source_issues: 191 line 4, 192 line 4 and 195 lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe and may be corrupt.

reading: Even seeing that all that grows on the branch, with its spreading red shoots and cool flowers, comes to die, they do not without fail praise our Lord's feet; when they are called, they will not know.
nuance: அழைக்கின்ற போது (when they are called) is the summons of death. அறியார் may mean they will not know what to do, or will not know him then, having not praised him before.

reading: A field ripened for five, and the five keep guard over that field; because a summons comes from the master of the five, the five gave up guarding the field.
nuance: The field is the body and the five are traditionally the senses, as in 151. The master of the five (ஐவர்க்கு நாயகன்) may be the life, or the Lord or Death who sends the ஓலை (palm-leaf summons); the verse does not say.

reading: There is one drum and there are two cymbals, and the king who lives within is there; when the king who lives within goes out, the drum becomes clay and lies dazed.
nuance: The drum is the body and the king the life. The two cymbals are not explained; the two breaths or the two legs are guesses. மண்ணாய் (becoming clay) recalls the clay pots of 143 and 158.

reading: Those who don't know the skill of calling it Venkatam do not know the precious life they could bear: the lord of Venkatam, the dancer of Vedanta, Nandi who plays within Venkatam.
nuance: வேங்கடம் is the name of the sacred hill, but here it is traditionally broken as வேம் கடம் (the pot that burns, the body), so that Nandi plays within the body. விரகு (skill, the trick of it) suggests the name is a key to be understood. The verse is obscure and the wordplay reading is tradition's, not the verse's own statement.

reading: People do not know that the sun, travelling all ten directions, measures out their lives by its knowing; the people of this earth do not stop and perceive it: this is the illusion that holds them, though they know of perishing.
nuance: The sun as the measure of life repeats 184. Line 4 (பொன்றுணர்வாரிற் புணர்க்கின்ற மாயம்) is hard to construe; it may say that maya binds even those who know they must die.

reading: No one has fully grasped that the strip of cloth, trimmed straight and bordered, will tear; you who see black hair turn white, say that end and birth lie within a single year.
nuance: பட்டிகை (a strip, a border, or a written record) is taken as the body or the allotted life. The last line (ஈறும் பிறப்பும் ஓராண்டு) is unclear: perhaps that birth and death are as close as one year to the next.

reading: For the pot with its ladle there is one measure of rice, and for the three hearth stones five firebrands; give out the rice before it burns too close; the days let go have already passed on.
nuance: A riddle. The pot is commonly read as the body, the three stones and five brands as inner fires and the senses. On the plain reading the verse urges giving food while it can be given; a yogic reading is also traditional and I can't fix it.

reading: As a bee that delights here goes to clusters of flowers and drinks their scented honey, so with the state of the life: even if one seeks it with joy and thinks of it, the one who stands in thought beyond the eye of the three lights does not stay within.
nuance: மூன்றொளி (three lights) are traditionally sun, moon and fire, and in yoga three centres of the body. Who does not stay (நில்லான்) is unclear: the life, which moves on like the bee, or the Lord beyond sight. The verse resists a confident reading.

reading: Considering how things are ordained to come, do good; considering how this earth is ordained to pass, praise the Pure One; if people ask why we need a destiny, it belongs to those able to win the rare gift of a good one.
nuance: விதி (ordinance, destiny) runs through every line, set against what one does: ஆம் விதி (what will come) and போம் விதி (what will pass). Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe and this reading is tentative.

reading: Do not stand speaking with envy so that virtue is ruined; do not turn harsh and snatch others' goods; be upright, and when you sit to eat well, give a ladleful first, when you have come into plenty.
nuance: அவ்வியம் (envy) and செவ்வியன் (the upright) are the same pair the Kural sets side by side in 169. தவ்வி is a ladle; the gift asked is small and constant, given at every meal.

title: கொல்லாமை
theme: Not killing (கொல்லாமை) is the finest offering in worship, and those who order killing are dragged to hell.
structure_note: Two verses: the first puts not killing at the head of inner worship, the second gives the punishment of those who urge killing.

reading: In worship of the good guru one clings to, among the many flowers the bright one is not killing other small lives; with it go the good garland, the unwavering lamp and the mind, and the place where the life settles is the crown of the head.
nuance: The verse turns the items of ritual worship (flower, garland, lamp) into inner ones, with not killing as the flower. அணுக்கள் may be small creatures or, in Siddhanta usage, souls. உச்சி is traditionally taken as the crown of the head where the yogi's awareness rests; a plainer reading of the last line isn't clear to me.

reading: Those brutish people who urged 'kill! stab!' are bound with strong ropes by Death's mighty servants, driven on with 'go! stop!', and made to stand in fire-mouthed hell.
nuance: The guilt falls on those who said 'kill' (கூறிய மாக்களை), not only on those who struck; the commands of the guilty are echoed back to them by Yama's servants ('go', 'stop', 'stay').

title: புலால் மறுத்தல்
theme: Refusing flesh (புலால் மறுத்தல்): those who eat flesh are thrown into hell, and those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying and reach Siva's feet are free of them in the bliss of knowledge.

reading: Those vile ones who eat foul flesh are seized by Yama's messengers in sight of all, flung on their backs into fire-mouthed hell and broken.
nuance: புலையர், a word for the lowest outcastes, is used here for flesh-eaters, so baseness is a matter of what one eats rather than one's birth. செல்லாக in the third line is obscure: 'as they go', or perhaps 'like a thunderbolt'; the sense of the verse doesn't depend on it.

reading: Killing, theft, lust and lying are sins as great as mountains; those who give them up, reach Siva's feet, which are the highest, and the joy there, have none of these, and that is the holy state of the bliss of knowledge.
nuance: The chapter is on refusing flesh, but this verse widens it to a list of great sins in which killing comes first and flesh-eating is not named. The last line makes freedom from the sins a mark of the state reached, not only a precondition for it.

title: பிறன்மனை நயவாமை
theme: Not desiring another man's wife (பிறன்மனை நயவாமை): a man who leaves his own wife for another's trades a sweet fruit for a poor one and falls; and even the learned and the yogis, once deluded by women, cannot turn the mind back.
structure_note: Two fruit images (201, 202) for the folly of leaving one's wife for another's, then a verse (203) on how even the accomplished fall to delusion.
source_issues: 203: line 3 reads மருள்கொணட, a misprint for மருள்கொண்ட.

reading: Young men who lust after another's guarded wife while their own wife is at home are like someone who won't eat the ripe jackfruit and toils for the fruit of the wild date.
nuance: The image weighs effort against reward: a large, sweet fruit already at hand against a small fruit from a thorny palm. ஆத்த, of one's own wife, is an unusual form; it is usually taken as 'married' or 'one's own'.

reading: Those who don't grasp the point hide away the sweet mango they tended and raised as if it were a treasure, then climb the branch of an ill-matched sour mango and fall and break their legs.
nuance: The sweet mango is the wife, kept locked in the house (அறையில் புதைத்து), and the sour tree another man's wife. The verse blames the man twice: for hoarding his own wife and for climbing elsewhere.

reading: Even the man who has grasped the meaning, those who command knowledge, and those who stand holding the flash of light in the darkness are infatuated with women who bewilder, and cannot change a mind once bewildered.
nuance: The three kinds of men are taken as the learned, the knowers and the yogis who see an inner light (இருள்கொண்ட மின்வெளி); that last phrase is a yogic term I can't fix. The verse speaks of women (மாதர்) in general, not only other men's wives, and its point is that attainment gives no protection.

title: மகளிர் இழிவு
theme: Against infatuation with women (மகளிர் இழிவு): their charm is like a fair-leaved poison tree, the pleasure is a dream and a whirlpool, their attachment shifts, and the sweetness at first turns bitter in the body.
structure_note: The chapter title speaks of women's baseness, but most verses describe the man's infatuation and its cost; 205 returns to other men's wives and 206 to fickle women.

reading: As the fruit of the etti tree cannot be eaten however good its leaves and clusters look, do not let your heart, which ought to turn away, burn for women who smile and display the beauty of their breasts.
nuance: The etti (strychnine tree) looks good and is poison, so the image is of an attractive surface over harm. The last line is unclear: வெய்துகொள்ளீர் may mean 'do not let it grow hot' or 'make it hard'; either way the heart is told to hold back.

reading: For men who enter a home seeking the wife there, the pleasure swirls them down like water in a deep pool; it seeps up like a dream and cannot be had as things are had awake.
nuance: Two images of the same pleasure: a whirlpool that drags one under, and a dream that leaves nothing. The grammar of the first two lines is loose, and I am not sure whether the whirling water is the pleasure or the woman.

reading: Women graceful as young she-elephants, though they cling like grass under a storm and say even the gods would be bewitched and bid a man stay near, turn to talk with strangers and are gone.
nuance: The middle lines are hard to construe; I take மயலுறும் வானவர் as the women's boast that even gods are enchanted by them. The point that survives any construal is the turn to others (அயலுறப் பேசி) and the leaving.

reading: Joining with young women in this world, the lot set for the body, is sweet cane juice from the press in the hand and turns to bitter neem within the body.
nuance: The contrast is in the place: sweet in the hand (கையகத்தே), bitter in the body (மெய்யகத்தே). The second line, மெய்யகத்தோடும் வைத்த விதியது, may mean that this is the fate attached to having a body; I am not sure of it.

reading: Weak-willed conduct is like wading to the middle of a moss-covered pond to sound its depth; unless such men are tied down and held back, they go the way of those who crawl into a narrow hole.
nuance: The moss-covered pond hides its depth, an image of danger under a smooth surface. பூழை is a narrow opening; it may be a plain trap image or a euphemism for the woman's body. The verse is obscure and my construal is tentative.

title: நல்குரவு
theme: Poverty (நல்குரவு) strips a man of livelihood, kin and standing; but the deeper want is a pit that goods cannot fill, filled only when impurity is gone, by praising the Lord and lighting the lamp of awareness.
structure_note: 209 describes worldly poverty; 210 and 211 turn it into the unfillable pit; 212 and 213 move from kin and the five senses to seeking the Lord.
source_issues: 212: line 4 reads தூர்க்கலு ம், a stray space in தூர்க்கலும்.

reading: The cloth is torn, the living is gone, even those who depended on him have turned unloving; for those who drift about the land there is no giving, no receiving, no festivity and no standing.
nuance: கோள் is taken as receiving, so the poor man is cut out of exchange both ways. நடை may be gait, standing or custom; I read it as standing among others.

reading: You who, as each dawn breaks, hunt for scarce goods to fill the false pit, praise the Lord whatever pit you fill; that pit is filled only when impurity is gone.
nuance: பொய்க்குழி, the false pit, is traditionally the belly, filled each day and empty again; it can also be read as the want that the body and its desires make. அழுக்கு is taken as the soul's impurity (மலம்). Both a plain and a spiritual reading of the pit stand.

reading: People seek even gold to fill the stony pit, and no one finds that easy; once one knows the understanding that fills it, the pit fills as impurity leaves.
nuance: கற்குழி may be a pit dug in rock, so hard to fill, or a play on கல்வி. The verse repeats 210 but names knowledge rather than praise as the way.

reading: The kin who cling and follow are worse than one's deeds; before the life departs, light the lamp of awareness while in the body, keep to it, and that road can be closed.
nuance: அவ்வழி may be the pit of 210 and 211 or the road of rebirth; கடந்தோர் in the second line is hard to construe. The claim that kin are worse than வினை is striking: kin hold one to the world as deeds do.

reading: The five senses, roaming like cattle over the paths, have inflicted endless suffering, and strong deeds have struck again and again; weary of such a life, he stood asking for the Lord.
nuance: The first line is obscure: அறுத்தன ஆறினும் ஆனினம் மேவி may be cattle grazing in cleared fields or on the six paths. ஐவர், 'the five', is traditionally the senses. The chapter's poverty here becomes the soul's.

title: அக்கினி காரியம்
theme: The fire rite (அக்கினி காரியம்): the Brahmins' oblation sustains sky, earth and gods and burns away deeds, and the Lord is within the sacrificial fire as the light in the heart.
structure_note: 214 to 220 speak of the outer rite and its fruits, with 216 to 218 turning toward an inner fire; 221 to 223 identify the fire with the Lord.
source_issues: 217: the verse is obscure throughout and may be corrupt; வேதிரண்டாகி and தாதிரண்டாகிய resist construal.
220: line 3 reads வருஞ்செல்வதது, a misprint for வருஞ்செல்வத்து.

reading: If steadfast Brahmins learned in the Veda pour the oblation, sky and earth, the quarters and the gods who rule them, and blameless great wealth all flourish.
nuance: The verse makes the rite a support of the whole world. விசையும் in the third line is unclear to me; it may be 'force' or 'speed'.

reading: The Brahmins who make the oblation seek the higher way, give to others before they eat, and reach the true path that the rule asks of them by their own understanding.
nuance: புறங்கொடுத்து உண்ணுவர can be 'eat after giving to others' or 'turn their backs and eat'; போகதி is unclear. I take the first reading, but it is a choice.

reading: For the Brahmins, the fire within the fire, and the inner meaning set within it, become, when it moves in the paired hours, a pure path that supports them.
nuance: அங்கியுள் அங்கி, the fire within the fire, is taken as an inner fire matching the outer one of the rite. இணைதுணை யாமம் may be the paired twilights or the paired breaths. I can't fix the sense.

reading: The verse speaks of reciting at two times and doing grace, of two that stand together in delight, and of cool birds that are two and grow heady; its sense is unclear.
nuance: Every line turns on 'two' (இரண்டு). Pairs like the two breaths, the two daily rites or Siva and Sakti are possible keys, but the verse doesn't name one, and I won't choose.

reading: For those who know how the tall flame fed by ghee reaches and burns the darkness, the darkness loosens that very day; and the wealth that lies in deeds becomes fire.
nuance: மை can be soot, darkness or blackness of the self; taken as impurity, the flame of the rite burns the soul's dark. The last line may mean that wealth gained by deeds is fuel for the fire or that it is itself harmful (தீயது, 'fire' or 'evil').

reading: As the wick laid in a wide lamp burns, the many ills of deeds lasting through ages fall away when the fire is worshipped and rises; the fire burns up deeds.
nuance: Deeds are called diseases (வினை நோய்), and the fire is their cure. வீழிசெய்து in the last line is obscure.

reading: Knowing great wealth to be ruin, they seek the Lord who made and gave the wealth to come, and, reckoning on the joy it will bring, they keep to the oblation, the rare wealth.
nuance: The verse sets two wealths against each other: the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) that ruins and the rare wealth (அருஞ்செல்வம்) of the rite. Which wealth 'the wealth to come' is, worldly or the joy beyond, isn't clear.

tamil: கண்சுட ரோன் உலகு ஏழும் கடந்த அத்
reading: The Lord who is bright flame and without end, who as that flame dwells in my heart, the light in the eye who passes beyond the seven worlds, is also the cool flame that heads the fire offering.
nuance: The verse joins three lights: the flame of the rite, the flame in the heart, and the light that passes beyond the worlds. 'Cool flame' (தண்சுடர்) is a deliberate paradox.

reading: Our Lord is in the fire of the oblation, and in the fire of the funeral pyre as the one who takes its essence; another fire yields the sea of deeds, and another is the roaring sea itself.
nuance: Four fires are named: ஓமம் (the rite), ஈமம் (the pyre), வேமம் and கோமம். The last two are obscure; கோமம் with the roaring sea may be the fire under the sea of Tamil tradition. My reading of lines 3 and 4 is a guess.

reading: The austere ones who tend the fire, who granted the way of abiding in the Veda, set it everywhere; and the great Lord, rising, establishes them: that is their glory.
nuance: The subject of the second half is unclear: the Lord may establish the fire or the ascetics. இளைப்ப is obscure.

title: அந்தண ரொழுக்கம்
theme: The conduct of Brahmins (அந்தணர் ஒழுக்கம்): a Brahmin is one who keeps the rites and through them reaches Vedanta, where craving ends; thread, tuft and birth without truth, knowledge and devotion don't make one.
structure_note: 224 to 227 describe the Brahmin by rite, mantra and Pranava; 228 to 233 redefine him by truth, freedom from craving and knowledge, with thread and tuft dismissed in 230 and the rites left behind in 232; 234 to 237 give the fruits for land, king and release.

reading: Brahmins are those who keep the six duties, tend the red fire, keep the rules at the three times of day, stand in good works, recite the twilight prayers, and so cut away ritual.
nuance: சடங்கறுப்போர் can mean those who complete the rites or those who end them; the second fits 232, where the rites are set aside, but the line doesn't settle it. The six duties are traditionally learning and teaching the Veda, sacrificing and having others sacrifice, giving and receiving.

reading: Brahmins are those who, eager to hear Vedanta, enter the Pranava in which the three states of knowing end, and see with joy the Lord who is the end of sound, of the Veda and of knowledge, without fixing any one thing as that end.
nuance: The verse stacks technical 'ends': நாதாந்தம் (end of sound), வேதாந்தம் (end of the Veda), போதாந்தம் (end of knowing). முப்பதம் may be the three letters of Om or three states. ஈதாந்தம் எனாது, 'not saying this is the end', refuses to stop at any one of them.

reading: The Vedic Brahmins are those glad to study the Gayatri and Savitri, who meditate on the mantra, ride the chariot of love into steady thought, and, become love itself, are not drowned in maya.
nuance: நேயம் (love, devotion) appears twice: as the chariot one rides and as what one becomes. The verse makes devotion the means of reciting the mantra rightly.

reading: The faultless Brahmins are those who grasp the Pranava, the great path, join the word through the guru's way, keep to the rites of the four Vedas, and become one with the true form.
nuance: சொரூபம், 'own form', is taken as the soul's true nature or Siva's; the verse doesn't say which.

reading: Truthfulness, austerity, becoming one with Him, wearing down the craving senses, knowing all lives as equal to oneself, and cutting off bondage: this is Brahman.
nuance: The verse defines பிரமம், the Brahmin's own word, by conduct. தானவன் ஆதலும் could be 'becoming He' or 'being a giver'; I take the first. ஒத்த உயிர்கள் means all lives seen as alike.

reading: Brahmins eager to hear Vedanta heard it and still kept their craving; but Vedanta is where craving ends, so those who have truly heard it have let craving go.
nuance: The verse plays வேதாந்தம் against வேட்கை (craving): the end of the Veda is the end of wanting. Hearing that leaves craving intact wasn't hearing.

reading: Are the sacred thread and the tuft Brahman? The thread is cotton and the tuft is hair; the real thread is Vedanta and the real tuft knowledge, as thread-wearing Brahmins would see if they looked.
nuance: The verse doesn't tell Brahmins to drop the thread; it says what the thread stands for. 241 goes further.

reading: Those mad fools without truth, without knowledge, without the sense that turns from the objects of the senses, without devotion and without knowing the Supreme are not Brahmins.
nuance: Five absences are listed and none of them is birth, so the verse denies the name to the born Brahmin who lacks them.

reading: For pure Brahmins, turiya samadhi is reaching the guru's feet by the guru's way, beyond the division of the conscious and the inert, and seeing once the rites and rules have been set aside.
nuance: துரியம் is the fourth state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; சித்தசித்து is the conscious and the inert. These are Siddhanta and Vedanta terms whose exact sense here I can't fix. The verse places the rites of 224 below the goal.

reading: Brahmins are truly such when their purity comes from the truth of Vedanta; knowing that what lacks it is mere noise, they know the Veda and are Brahmins.
nuance: The grammar of the second and third lines is loose; I take கோலாகலம் (noise, show) as the verdict on rite without Vedanta.

reading: The fertile land where Brahmins who wear cool kindness and meditate on the end of the Veda live does not decline and its king prospers; they make the oblation at dusk and dawn.
nuance: அந்தண்மை பூண்ட echoes the Kural's செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான் (Kural 30), the edition's own parallel. Here the Brahmin's virtue benefits the land and king.

reading: For those whose rule makes the knowledge of Vedanta shine, the course that approaches the awareness at the end of sound enters the Supreme beyond knowing, and so both release at the end of sound and powers are reached.
nuance: Again the verse stacks Vedanta, நாதாந்தம் and போதாந்தம், as technical stages. It promises both முத்தி (release) and சித்தி (powers) without ranking them.

reading: When the one and the two are brought together, those blessed with grace, however well they live and however many good things they speak, seek out and go to worship the Lord who shines victorious.
nuance: ஒன்றும் இரண்டும் is unexplained: it could be the soul and Siva, the self and its two bonds, or a number of breaths or syllables. The rest of the verse is clear: worship remains even for the accomplished.

reading: When the two attachments fall away of themselves, the self is let go and nothing is sought; then Brahma on his flower, enjoying merit, receives the single oblation of Om.
nuance: The two attachments are traditionally 'I' and 'mine'. The verse seems to make the giving up of self the true oblation, received by the gods; the third and fourth lines are hard to construe.

title: அரசாட்சி முறை (இராச தோடம்)
theme: The order of kingship (அரசாட்சி முறை): an unlearned king is worse than Death; the king must follow and guard the way of austerity, test and punish false holy men and the faithless, protect the helpless, and take his sixth.
structure_note: 238 and 239 on the king's own learning and conduct; 240 to 242 on false wearers of holy garb; 243 to 245 on protection and the king's share; 246 and 247 on punishing drinkers and those who break their faith's rules.
source_issues: 244: line 4 reads வேந்தனுககு, a misprint for வேந்தனுக்கு.

reading: An unlearned king and Death are alike, but Death is much the better: the unlearned king, blind to dharma, says 'kill', while Death does not come near the good.
nuance: The comparison turns on discrimination: Death spares the good, the unlearned king doesn't.

reading: If a king does not every day look to the way of austerity in his land and keep to it himself, the land declines daily, folly sets in, and his wealth shrinks day by day.
nuance: நாள்தோறும் opens every line: the king's duty and the land's decline are both daily.

reading: What use is the holy garb to those who don't live by it? For those who do, it is the true garb; and if a strong king makes those who don't live by it do so, that leads to release.
nuance: It isn't clear whose release (வீடு) is meant: the false ascetics' once corrected, or the king's for correcting them.

reading: If those whose ignorance remains take up the tuft and sacred thread, the land withers and even a great king loses his standing; so, on reflection, it is good to cut off this showy thread and tuft.
nuance: The verse doesn't name who cuts them off; in a chapter on kingship, the king is implied.

reading: When those without knowledge put on matted hair, tuft and thread and act the part of the wise, it is good for the land that the king test them through the wise and bring them to knowledge.
nuance: The remedy is correction, not only punishment: the king tests them through the wise and makes knowledge arise.

reading: If the king, whose task is to protect cows, women, the virtuous and the holy ones the gods honour, fails to protect them, unending hell awaits him in the next world.
nuance: பாவை (lit. doll, image) is taken as women. The punishment falls on the king himself, after death.

reading: If you want release and wealth, keep to the path of dharma without lapse even in forgetfulness; and of all that is produced in the well-watered world, the king's share, as is declared, is one sixth.
nuance: The one-sixth share is the traditional royal tax. மறந்தும் means 'even by forgetting', that is, never. The two halves are loosely joined; திறந்தரு may be 'that gives strength' or 'excellent'.

reading: When the king guards the world well, worthy people follow the same path; but one who comes to seize the world, for others or for himself, has the evil nature of a pouncing tiger.
nuance: The second half is hard to construe: போந்திவ் வுலகைப் பிறர்க்கொள்ளத் தாங்கொள்ள may describe a king who lets others plunder or plunders himself. My reading is tentative.

reading: It is the king's duty to punish those deluded people who drink liquor instead of drinking the nectar taken by binding the breath, raising the fire and holding the moon's face.
nuance: கால் (breath), கனல் (fire) and சோமன் (the moon) are yogic terms: the breath held, the inner fire raised, and the nectar from the moon at the crown, traditionally. The verse sets the yogi's inner drink against toddy (தேறல்).

reading: Those who don't keep to the proper rules of their own faith suffer every punishment in the next life under the Agama law spoken by Siva; to punish them truly in this life is the king's duty.
nuance: The verse divides punishment between the two worlds: Siva's Agama in the next, the king in this. Each faith is judged by its own rules (தத்தம் சமயத் தகுதி), not by one.

title: வானச் சிறப்பு
theme: The excellence of rain (வானச் சிறப்பு): rain flowing with nectar makes every tree, sweet and bitter, bear nectar, and the Lord's clear river springs within the heart like rain falling from a mountain.

reading: Through the great rain that flows with nectar, nectar-bearing trees spring up on earth, areca and coconut with sugarcane and banana; even the bitter kanjirai is fed by it.
nuance: The bitter kanjirai (strychnine tree) in the last line may be named to show that rain feeds all alike, or the line may say the bitter tree too yields nectar. The verse doesn't judge between sweet and bitter.

reading: Like a waterfall of rain descending from the mountain, my Father's clear river springs up within the heart, beyond words, foamless, stainless, fine and without banks.
nuance: The rain becomes an image of the Lord's grace inside the heart; the yogic tradition may also read the mountain as the head and the stream as nectar from the crown. Both a devotional and a yogic reading stand.

title: தானச் சிறப்பு
theme: The excellence of giving (தானச் சிறப்பு): give to anyone without discrimination, look for others before eating, don't hoard, and learn from the crow that calls its kin before it eats.

reading: Give to everyone without asking who they are; look out for others before you eat; don't hoard old goods; you who are hungry, don't hurry to eat alone; know the hour when the crow calls out and then eats.
nuance: Five commands in four lines, closing on the crow that calls its flock to food, an old Tamil image of sharing. அவரிவர் என்னன்மின், 'don't say this one or that one', rules out choosing worthy recipients.

title: அறஞ்செய்வான் திறம்
theme: The way of one who does virtue (அறஞ்செய்வான் திறம்): virtue is within everyone's reach, a leaf for God, a mouthful for a cow, a handful before eating, a kind word; it must be done before Death comes, and austerity and virtue are the boat across the sea of deeds.
structure_note: What those who know themselves become (251); small acts anyone can do and feeding the needy (252, 253); urgency before death (254 to 257); austerity and virtue as boat and support (258, 259).
source_issues: 259: line 3 (உற்று உங்களால் ஒன்றும் ஈந்தது வே துணை) is metrically and grammatically broken; வே may be a fragment.
257: line 1 (தான்தவம் செய்வதாம் செய்தவத்து அவ்வழி) is obscure.

reading: Those who know themselves bow at the Lord's feet, stand upholding virtue and become the few who know the real; to such people the Supreme becomes their own kin.
nuance: தாமறிவார் opens every line. It is read here as 'those who know themselves', but it can also be 'they who know (this)'. தத்துவர் is taken as knowers of the tattvas, the real constituents; தமர் (one's own people) makes the Supreme a kinsman rather than a distant judge.

reading: Anyone can give a green leaf to God, a mouthful of grass to a cow, a handful of food to another before eating, and a kind word to others.
nuance: யாவர்க்குமாம், 'possible for all', is the verse's argument: each act is tiny, so no one can plead poverty. Worship, care of animals, sharing food and speech are set side by side as equal forms of virtue.

reading: Men fragrant with learned wisdom say that the food eaten by those who have nothing is virtue; those who do not feed them do not know the merit, as of one whose well or tank people come to and drink from.
nuance: அற்றுநின்றார் can be the destitute or those who have cut off attachment, the renunciants. Lines 3 and 4 are compressed; the reading that the giver's merit is like that of one who dug a public well is traditional but not stated outright.

reading: You who neither drive out your impurity and fill yourselves with knowledge nor do good while your days are full, what will you do when you lie awake as fever spreads, and what when your eyes no longer open, poor hearts?
nuance: விழித்திருந்து and விழிக்க அன்று frame the deathbed: sleepless in the last fever, then unable to open the eyes. அழுக்கு (dirt) may be inner impurity in the sense of malam, but the verse does not use the technical word. தழுக்கிய நாள் is taken as days of plenty.

reading: Before Death comes in force, which does not ask whether you know yourself, whether you are good, whether you are poor or young, do good austerity in its proper way.
nuance: The four negated verbs in lines 1 and 2 can describe Death, which takes no account of who one is, or the hearer, who goes on without knowing himself. Either way youth is no excuse for delay.

reading: For one who has renounced there is no kin from then on, for one who has died no joy, and to one who has forgotten him the Lord has not come; those who know the measure of knowing know virtue.
nuance: வழிமுதல் (from that point on) marks three things that end at a moment: kinship at renunciation, joy at death, the Lord's coming at forgetting. The last line can also be read 'virtue itself knows those who know the measure'.

reading: Those who in their austerity honour the deer-bearing Lord as God are set against the many beings who live taking the flesh as their god; to them Yama comes, saying 'I am god'.
nuance: மான் is taken as the deer Siva holds, so 'the deer-bearer' is Siva; line 1 is obscure. The plain point is ironic: those who serve the body get Death (நமன்) as the god who claims them.

reading: There are two ways that end weariness and are a boat across the surging sea of deeds: austerity and virtue, which the Lord of unfailing renown makes fruitful, are the highest support for oneself and one's kin.
nuance: கேடில் புகழோன் may be the Lord or the man of lasting fame who practises the two. The sea is of deeds (வினைக்கடல்), the stuff that keeps births going.

reading: The Lord, the support worth clinging to, does not tell the secret of release on earth except to those on the path of virtue; whatever you have given will be your help, and that is the way to take the path he set.
nuance: பற்றது வாய்நின்ற பற்று plays on பற்று (attachment, support) as Kural 350 does. அற்றம் can mean a secret, an end or release; line 3 (உற்று உங்களால் ஒன்றும் ஈந்தது வே துணை) is broken and the sense is a guess.

title: அறஞ்செயான் திறம்
theme: The way of one who does not do virtue (அறஞ்செயான் திறம்): the hoarder's wealth is poison fruit, the unvirtuous see bodies perish and still learn nothing, disease and hell await them; joy and sorrow come from past deeds, so give and praise the Lord instead of flattering the rich.
structure_note: Wasted wealth and wasted days (260, 261); what the unvirtuous lack and suffer (262 to 266); joy and sorrow as the fruit of deeds, and the call to give and worship (267 to 269).
source_issues: 260: line 3 reads கொணடு, a misprint for கொண்டு.
265: மழிநடக்கும் in line 3 is obscure and may be corrupt.
268: line 4 (பசுவது வாமே) is obscure.

reading: The wealth of those who do no clinging good is like the large fruit of the poisonous etti that ripens and falls; base wretches who heap it up by lending at interest and scoop it into the ground do not know what it is for.
nuance: எட்டி is the strychnine tree, whose fruit looks ripe but cannot be eaten. ஒட்டிய நல்லறம் is taken as virtue that stays with one beyond death. Usury (வட்டி) is singled out as the way such wealth is gathered.

reading: The ages have gone, aeons have passed, plans have run out and the days grow short; even seeing bodies, sources of great affliction, destroyed as if wrung out, they do not know virtue.
nuance: கற்பனை may be imaginings and plans, or kalpa, the aeon, echoing ஊழி in line 1. பிழிந்தன போல (as if squeezed) gives the body as something wrung dry.

reading: Those who do not know virtue do not know how to think of the Lord's feet and do not know even the outskirts of Siva's city; many of them, listening to false words, know only wrongdoing and stay fixed in enmity.
nuance: மறம் here is the opposite of அறம், wrongdoing, not the martial valour it means in war poetry. The chain runs from not knowing virtue to not knowing the Lord: ethics comes first.

reading: Cough, wasting, phlegm and fever belong to those who do not do good; thunderbolt, snake, rohini and tumour do not come near those who do.
nuance: The verse makes virtue a literal protection against illness and mishap. உரோணி is unclear: a disease of the throat in some lists, or the star Rohini as an evil influence.

reading: You do not praise the Supreme who is to be praised, do not give even a little to those who beg, do not water and raise groves with a pot; will you stand in hell, good-hearted ones?
nuance: The groves (கா) are taken as flower gardens kept for worship. நல்நெஞ்சினீரே may be ironic or a sincere appeal to people capable of better. ஈதலை யாயினும் is unclear; read as 'even a little'.

reading: Those who stray from the path go back into the womb, while those who keep to it, driving off the stain of deeds, stand high; without walking the path no one reaches the world of the gods.
nuance: The verse plays on வழி (path) and கழி (going astray). கருப்பு ஆரும் is read as entering the womb again; மழிநடக்கும் is obscure and the reading of lines 1 to 3 is a guess at the plain contrast.

reading: Those who have ripened see the Lord's feet, the resolute rule his heaven, but the swollen-headed die without a single support, fallen into a withering anger.
nuance: கனிந்தவர் (ripened, softened) is commonly taken as those mellowed in love, துணிந்தவர் as those who boldly renounced, மலிந்தவர் as those swollen with wealth or pride. மெலிந்த சினம் is obscure.

reading: Joy and sorrow, the two, are settled by what one did before; fools who see joy and still do not give, loveless in mind, do not know virtue.
nuance: The argument is from cause: present joy is the fruit of past good, so withholding now spends it without renewal. Lack of giving is traced to lack of love (அன்பிலார்).

reading: The Lord of unfailing renown decides ruin and gain and will not let you seek pleasure by doing what is unfair; think of offering and giving, and if you do what brings joy it will be like a cow that yields.
nuance: இடுவதும் ஈவதும் may be offering (to God or fire) and giving (to people). பசுவது வாமே is obscure: a cow that keeps giving milk, or பசு in the Siddhanta sense of the bound soul.

reading: Do not wither praising petty-minded men for their wealth in hope of a living; with your true home in mind, praise the Lord, as an archer fixes his mark to hit the target.
nuance: இல்லம் கருதி may mean thinking of one's household or of the final home with the Lord. Line 1 (சிலர்பலர் வாழ்வெனும்) is compressed. The archer image asks for a single aim.

title: அன்புடைமை
theme: Having love (அன்புடைமை): love and Siva are not two; austerity without melting love cannot reach him, but he stands in the love of those who praise him, dwells within love, and is the near support of those who live in it.
structure_note: The thesis that love is Siva (270); the poet's own love and its answer (271, 274, 275); love against austerity (272) and against mere desire (278); Siva within love (276, 277, 279).
source_issues: 273: line 4 (கோர நெறிகொடு கொங்குபுக்காரே) is obscure.
276: line 3 (வன்படைத்து இந்த அகலிடம் வாழ்வினில்) is unclear.

reading: The ignorant say love and Siva are two; no one knows that love itself is Siva; once they know it, they rest as love that is Siva.
nuance: அன்பே சிவம் is the verse's refrain and one of the best-known lines in Tamil. The last line makes knowing it transformative: those who know do not merely hold a doctrine but sit (அமர்ந்திருந்தார்) as that love.

reading: My great love is entwined with the one who wears the tiger skin that outshines gold, with the young crescent gleaming like lightning, who bathes in the ash heaped close about him.
nuance: The tiger skin, crescent and burning-ground ash (சுடுபொடி) are Siva's standard marks. கிடந்து runs through the lines, so the love lies close to him as the skin, moon and ash do.

reading: Even if one makes one's bones the firewood, cuts one's flesh and fries it in the fire till it glows like gold, none but those who melt with love and soften within can reach my gem.
nuance: The extreme of bodily austerity is set aside in favour of love that melts (உருகி) and softens (குழை). என்போல் மணி is unclear: 'my gem' or 'the gem that is like me'.

reading: Those with longing see Hara, those with tenderness see his feet, but those who carry a burden see only birth, as if they had taken a harsh road into Kongu.
nuance: ஆர்வம், ஈரம், பாரம் rhyme as three states of the heart; பாரம் is taken as the weight of attachment or deeds, and பவம் as birth. Line 4 (கோர நெறிகொடு கொங்குபுக்காரே) is obscure: கொங்கு may be the Kongu country, or honey.

reading: Melt your love and praise the Lord; melt your love first and seek the First One; when I later melted with love, great Nandi made his love for me stand foremost.
nuance: என் அன்பு, முன் அன்பு, பின் அன்பு, தன் அன்பு move from the hearer's love to the Lord's answering love. Nandi is Tirumular's teacher and also a name of Siva; the verse need not choose.

reading: Even if one praises him only once as the self-born, he stands then as a companion on the way to heaven; Siva, wearing the konrai with honey on one side, stood in my love in a way all his own.
nuance: ஒரு runs through the lines (ஒரு காலம், ஒரு பால், ஒரு வண்ணம்): a single praise is enough to make him a companion. சயம்பு is svayambhu, the self-born.

reading: People do not know how to hold with love our Lord, the First who first created and created joy; yet he who locked love into life in this wide world stays in his own wide realm.
nuance: அடைத்து (locking in, enclosing) is used twice: people fail to enclose the Lord in love, while he enclosed love in the world. வன்படைத்து and the second அகலிடம் are unclear.

reading: If one sets in the mind the Lord who shines like the sun of fine red gold, keeps him there, praises him as Lord and seeks his grace with longing, the king of the gods grants increase.
nuance: அருத்தி is longing or devotion. விருத்தி can be growth, livelihood or, in later usage, growth in grace; the verse does not say which.

reading: Though they know the order set by the one who made daily sleep and birth, men keep him within their wants, calling him 'our father, our Lord', and do not seek him with longing.
nuance: நித்தலும் துஞ்சும் பிறப்பு may be 'daily sleep and birth' or 'the birth that daily dies'; sleep as a small death is an old figure (Kural 339). The complaint is that people call on the Lord for what they want (இச்சை) rather than out of love for him (நச்சி).

reading: He is within love and outside it, within the body, before and after, lord even of the sages; the rare being who dwells within love is a close support only to those who dwell in love.
nuance: அன்பின் உள் occurs four times. The Lord is everywhere (inside, outside, before, after), yet his nearness as support (அணைதுணை) is given only to those in love.

title: அன்பு செய்வாரை அறியும் சிவன்
theme: Siva knows those who love him (அன்பு செய்வாரை அறியும் சிவன்): he sees what each has spurned and gained and returns love with grace; siddhas cannot find him but he stands before devotees; claims to know him through love ring hollow without true understanding, and mingling with him inwardly is the true worship.
structure_note: Grace answering love (280 to 282); union with him as lovers' union (283); devotees against siddhas and against false claims (284, 286, 287); the poet's vision and inner worship (285, 288, 289).

reading: The Lord knows what we have spurned and what we have gained; the excellent Lord gives grace gladly, and to those who can love with tender, fresh love so that grace grows, his grace returns their love with delight.
nuance: கொழுந்தன்பு is love like a young shoot, fresh and growing. The chapter's title idea opens here: the Lord knows (அறியும்), so love is not unseen.

reading: Though the Lord made what suits a joyful birth and the toils of a sorrowful birth are many, this birth that the First Lord ordained by mingling in love is where births end.
nuance: அன்பிற் கலவிசெய்து (mingling in love) and முன்பு இப்பிறவி are compressed. One reading is that a birth lived in love with the Lord is the last birth; முடிவது may also mean simply 'is fulfilled'.

reading: The light that rises above a loving mind consents to accept the joyful garland; free of the tangle of the five sorrowful snares, seek the mind that is friendly to him.
nuance: கண்ணி means both garland and snare, and the verse uses both: the joyful garland of love offered to him, and the five snares that dance, traditionally the senses.

reading: For those who can subside into feeling as love settles on a woman in union, the joy of embracing him, delighting and moving beyond awareness, is like that.
nuance: Sexual union is the image for union with the Lord. உணர்ச்சியில்லாது (without awareness) is taken as loss of separate self-awareness. அதுவிது (that is this) leaves open which joy is the measure of the other.

reading: The siddhas, even with those close to him, have never discerned that fitting light; but to devotees who bowed and worshipped him in devotion he stood before them and gave release.
nuance: பத்திமை is bhakti, devotion. The contrast is pointed in a book that elsewhere honours siddhas: attainment does not find him, devotion does. உற்றுநின்றாரொடும் is unclear.

reading: I saw the feet of him with fragrant konrai, the twin anklets of him who wears the elephant's hide, the feet of him who dwells in the lotus; I saw the anklet within my love.
nuance: கண்டேன் opens every line. The one dwelling in the lotus is usually Brahma, but here may be Siva in the heart-lotus; the last line places the vision inside the poet's love.

reading: No one knows the Lover: Nambhan, whom the gods above hail as the leader who becomes things of many kinds, the joyful one who abides in joy and relishes it.
nuance: அன்பன் can be 'the one who loves' or 'the one loved'. இரதிக்கும் (relishes) gives the Lord himself as enjoying joy.

reading: Those who do not know their past births and deaths say 'we know the Lord through love', but they cannot know in love Nandi, who is joy and has no birth or death.
nuance: The verse sets the claimants' bondage to birth and death against Nandi's freedom from it. Whether it rejects their claim outright or says love alone is not enough without knowledge of bondage is unclear.

reading: The Lord knows those who night and day keep themselves in the bond and show him tender care; if they abide radiant and cease from action, the Lord comes and stands gathered among us.
nuance: பாசத்துள் வைத்து may mean in the bond of love, or, in Siddhanta language, while still in the fetters (பாசம்) that bind the soul. செயலற்றிருந்திடில் (becoming actionless) is taken as surrender or yogic stillness.

reading: Why let go of the excellent light and then grasp it again? I will hold to his endless greatness and follow it; to mingle in honey with the Lord who stands as my life is the sacred bath.
nuance: மஞ்சனம் is the ritual bathing of the image; the verse makes inner union the true ablution. மட்டு may be honey (of love) or measure, giving 'mingling without measure'.

title: கல்வி
theme: Learning (கல்வி): true learning is learning to hold the Lord. It brings him into the heart, gives the learned an eye, cuts away sin when joined to worship, and goes with one as a companion, while clinging to one text or faction in delusion, or having no learning, leaves one without support.
structure_note: The poet's own learning (290); learning as sight and as worship (291, 292); learning as companion and ladder (294, 296); the failures of partial or absent learning (295, 297); cling to the Lord (298) who dwells in open hearts (299). 293 is obscure.
source_issues: 293: lines 1 and 2 (கல்வியுடையார் கழிந்தோடிப் போகின்றார் / பல்லியுடையார் பாம்பரிந்து உண்கின்றார்) are obscure and may be corrupt.
291: line 4 (கற்றறி காட்டக் கயல்உள வாக்குமே) is obscure.
297: lines 2 and 3 (கழித்துணை, ஒழித்துணை) are unclear.

reading: I came to know the sign by which body and life are joined and how to hold fast the Lord of the gods; he came unhindered and entered my heart, and I learned a learning that surpasses.
nuance: குறிப்பு (sign, hidden meaning) is read as the secret of how life holds to the body, which tradition takes yogically. கறிப்பறியா in line 4 is obscure; it may mean learning that knows no lack or no bitterness.

reading: When the learned reflect, there is an eye within their thought, and what they say after reflecting, their learning reveals, gives clear sight.
nuance: கற்றறிவாளர் repeats in three lines. Line 4 (கற்றறி காட்டக் கயல் உளவாக்குமே) is obscure; கயல் (carp) is a stock comparison for the eye, so the line may say learning makes seeing eyes.

reading: While you still stand, learn to serve the feet of the Steady One and your sins will fall away and be cut off; worship without failing in word, and once you have, he becomes a gem lamp with no second.
nuance: Learning is here something done with the Lord's feet: study and worship are one act. நிற்கின்ற போதே is taken as 'while alive'. The gem lamp (மணிவிளக்கு) gives a light that needs no oil.

reading: The learned pass away and are gone, and those with the lizard eat cut snakes; but if you praise the Lord night and morning, the body becomes as if transmuted by alchemy in the herb.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure; பல்லி may be lizard (with its omens) or a form of பல் (tooth). வாதித்த is taken from வாதம் (alchemy) and வல்லி as a herb, so the claim may be that worship makes the body lasting where learning alone does not.

reading: Pure good light comes as a companion, pure good word comes as a companion, pure good fragrance comes as a companion, pure good learning comes as a companion.
nuance: The four lines are parallel and the verse does not say how light, word, fragrance and learning relate. Read in the chapter, learning is the last and summing item; the light, word and fragrance may be taken symbolically (the Lord, mantra, the scent of worship).

reading: Those who hold to one text and cannot climb to its end, or cling to one side and lose the fruit of good nature, are like birds scattered at one raised stick: holding to one delusion, they are bewildered.
nuance: The verse puns on ஒன்று பற்றி (holding one thing) four times. நூல் is thread and book, பால் milk or side (faction). The reading against narrow, sectarian learning is a guess at a compressed verse.

reading: To those who search, Hara appears right there; the fire within sheds the light of a pure gem; and for those who can reach the young crescent, it becomes a thread-ladder for the ready mind.
nuance: நூலேணி puns on rope ladder and ladder of texts. இளமதி may be the crescent on Siva's head or the moon centre of yogic practice; நெருப்பு and மணி may also be yogic. The plain sense is that study, rightly used, leads up to him.

reading: Before the Lord who was companion on the way and medicine, the mind of the unlearned is cast aside; he of great nature, the one above, is the companion on the way through all seven worlds.
nuance: வழித்துணை and மருந்து are epithets of Siva; Sengalvaraya notes Sundarar's 'வழித்துணை மருந்தே' (Tevaram 7.70.9). கழித்துணை and ஒழித்துணை are unclear.

reading: If you would cling, cling to the Supreme; with the First One's grace all is fulfilled, and the learned, by the skill they have, stand in great bliss like the shining gods.
nuance: பற்றது பற்றில் plays on பற்று as Kural 350 does: attachment redirected, not abolished. கிற்ற விரகு (the skill one has) is unclear, and so is whether the shining gods are a comparison or what the learned become.

reading: He who owns the sea and the mountain, whose body is the five elements, the lord of the immortals who rides the mighty bull through age after age, dwells in the hearts of those who have room for him.
nuance: இடமுடையார் is those with room in their hearts; it may also pun on those who own land. The Lord who owns the sea and mountains chooses the heart as his dwelling.

title: கேள்வி கேட்டமைதல்
theme: Being settled by listening (கேள்வி கேட்டமைதல்): hearing about the Lord, his deeds and his grace, then reciting and realising it, leads to the Siva-state and makes people like gods; but what counts is knowing him with longing, not hearing or reckoning alone.
structure_note: The chapter opens with the kinds of hearing that end in Siva-gati (300) and the order recite, listen, realise (301); it then promises godhood and grace to those who hear and speak of him (302 to 305), sets listening among the soul's supports (307), and closes on those for whom hearing is empty (306, 308, 309).

reading: Hearing of virtue, hearing the words of the andhanar, hearing of wrong, hearing the mantras of the gods, hearing of outer things, and hearing the ways of our gold-bodied Lord: by these the Siva-state is gained.
nuance: The repeated கேட்டும் can be additive (by all these hearings) or concessive (though one hears all these, it is hearing the Lord's ways that gains the goal). மறம் is taken as wrong, the opposite of அறம், or as valour; புறம் as outer or worldly matters, or other doctrines.

reading: Who knows the Lord of the gods, the divine form? Once you know him, recite, listen and realise; those who recited and realised stood exalted.
nuance: ஓதுமின் கேள்மின் உணர்மின் puts the three in order: recitation, listening, realisation, the last being the point. The first two lines can also be read 'whoever knows him'.

reading: If great Nandi wills, one hears Mayan's word; one hears Brahma's word through Hara's will; those who hear Siva's word become gods; to hear the word that bears fruit is the real hold.
nuance: பணி may be word, command or service. மயன் may be Maya the divine artificer or Vishnu (மாயன்). பற்று in the last line may be the refuge one holds to or, negatively, attachment; I read it as refuge, but the line is unclear.

reading: Holy people who stay saying of him 'this is the Lord' will later become gods; our First Lord, of rare tapas, gladly grants grace to the great ascetics who come to him.
nuance: The first half rewards speech about the Lord, the second tapas. அருமாதவத்து can describe the Lord or the tapas through which the ascetics come.

reading: Speaking of the Lord's grace, of death and of birth, babbling in delight, he becomes love to them and, standing as the living light, abides like the scent in a fragrant flower.
nuance: பிதற்றி, babbling, is praise here: the talk of the enraptured devotee. The subject shifts between the devotees and the Lord; the scent in the flower is an image of his presence, felt and unseen.

reading: When the mind grasps excellence, listening and the conduct of true knowledge, if it does not slip from them, one becomes, without fault, even the king of the gods for countless ages.
nuance: The last two lines are compressed: the one who holds fast may become the king of the gods, or the king of the gods may stay with him. வழுக்கி and இழுக்கு both carry the sense of slipping.

reading: Like children who belch over rice made of sand, those who think enjoyment of the Real comes by mere closeness, and who do not fix on the One that cannot be fixed, have stayed without knowing; they are not what they claim.
nuance: The sand-rice of children's play is food that cannot satisfy. குறியாதது, what cannot be marked or made an object, is traditionally the Supreme beyond every sign. செறிவு may be closeness, crowding or accumulation; the target of the verse is unclear beyond its mockery of pretended experience.

reading: Life and body are a close support; listening that reaches the world is a close support; the mind on Siva's feet is the firm support; if one seeks the support to be gained, there is no birth.
nuance: A graded list of supports, each repeating துணை: the bodily, the learned, and the mind fixed on Siva, which alone ends birth. The verse does not despise the first two.

reading: Our Lord, the Ancient One, is there for those who praise him; for those who scorn him he becomes the place of suffering; and for those who stand apart, not reciting and knowing the First with joy, he is a cow of stone.
nuance: A stone cow looks like a cow and gives no milk. Read with the dative, the Lord is that to those who stand apart; it is also possible to read the stone cow as the people themselves.

reading: Though one holds him in mind, speaks him aloud and knows him in accord, though forms do not match one another, and though the axle turns and the pin is shaken, the First comes near only to those who know him with longing.
nuance: The axle and linchpin (அச்சு, ஆணி) are often taken as the body as a cart failing at death; நச்சு is longing, though it can also mean poison. The lines before the last are obscure, and the verse may be saying that mind and speech alone are not enough.

title: கல்லாமை
theme: Lack of learning (கல்லாமை), where learning means knowing Siva: the unlearned take the passing for the lasting, cannot see the Lord in their hearts and suffer their deeds, while those who know the true reckoning have truly learned; book learning without Siva-knowledge or love is itself a kind of unlearning.
structure_note: The chapter keeps turning the word கல்லாதார்: the unlearned who see by grace (310) and the poet's own unlearning (313) stand beside the unlearned who cannot see the Lord (311, 312, 314, 317), and the learned who lack Siva-knowledge (315, 318, 319). 316 defines the truly learned as those who know the கணக்கு.
source_issues: 310 and 313 are hard to construe; 313 line 1 (கில்லேன்) may be corrupt.

reading: Even the unlearned, if skilled in the vision that knows the meaning, are valued by the eye of grace; the unlearned hold to the truth, and even the learned cannot see the joy of the unlearned.
nuance: The verse is hard to construe. பற்றா நிற்பர் can mean 'stand holding' or 'stand not holding' the truth, and the last line can mean that the learned cannot see the joy of the unlearned or that the learned, like the unlearned, do not see joy. Against the rest of the chapter it seems to allow a graced unlearning that sees what learning misses.

reading: The able always live joined to the one way, while the others say knowledge is many; our God is in every place, but the unlearned do not know his being mingled in all.
nuance: வல்லார், the able, stands for the truly learned. அறிவு பல, 'knowledge is many', is taken as the many doctrines of the sects. கலப்பு may be his pervasion of all or the soul's union with him.

reading: You who feel in your heart that the state which does not stay is lasting, and that this perishing hut is permanent: though he is the Lord of all lives, he cannot be seen in the hearts of the unlearned.
nuance: குரம்பை, a hut or nest, is the body. The verse ties lack of learning to one specific error, taking the impermanent for the lasting.

reading: I could not; I fell into the delusion that makes the suffering of deeds; I did not learn, being one who did not know Hara's way; yet with the Giver in my mind, I, unlearned, can go beyond and dance.
nuance: A first-person confession whose turn is from கல்லேன் (I did not learn) to வல்லேன் (I am able). I take 'the Giver' (வழங்கும் பொருள்) as the Lord whose grace makes up what learning did not; ஆடவல்லேன் may echo the Lord's name ஆடவல்லான், the dancer. The first word கில்லேன் and the second line's syntax are uncertain.

reading: Thinking that life does not stay and is not lasting, the able have entered virtue and tapas; the unlearned men, the base of the world, live out the suffering of evil deeds.
nuance: The able here act on impermanence, by virtue and austerity; the unlearned simply undergo it. கயவர், the base, is the word of the Kural's chapter on baseness.

reading: The shining fruit that ripened within the sky was mingled within the eye and stayed there; yet those within the earth reckoned and reckoned, thought and wrote, and wore themselves out.
nuance: The plain point is that what scholars seek in books is already near. Traditionally the sky is the inner space at the crown, the eye the point between the brows, and the fruit Siva's light seen in yoga; the verse does not say so, and both readings stand.

reading: It cannot be seen except by those who know the reckoning, and the vision is not won except by them; knowing the reckoning, they see the truth and stand to reach it; those who know the reckoning are the ones who have learned.
nuance: கணக்கு, the word repeated in every line, means account, measure or method; it is traditionally taken as the right order of knowing (of the tattvas, or of the path), not arithmetic. அண்ட நிற்கும் is unclear: perhaps 'stand near', perhaps 'stand in the cosmos'.

reading: One should not even look upon unlearned fools, nor is it one's duty to hear their words; beside unlearned fools the merely unlearned are good; unlearned fools do not know the meaning.
nuance: The third line separates the unlearned fool (கல்லாத மூடர்) from the plainly unlearned, who are better. It can also be read 'to unlearned fools, the unlearned seem good', that is, fools prize their own kind.

reading: Wretches who have learned yet lack Siva-knowledge do not leave their kin or rid themselves of fault; they are fools, and the witless do not see the many directions; those who stand in love after learning are the ones who know the reckoning.
nuance: The chapter's sharpest claim: learning without சிவஞானம் leaves one among the fools. சுற்றமும் வீடார் may also pun on வீடு, release. The last line joins love to learning and recalls 316's கணக்கறிந்தார்.

reading: He is the First Lord, the supreme flame even to the immortals, the great god whom the devotees of light follow; people say 'we can recite and know him', but they do not know the course of the light that stands within and moves them.
nuance: சோதி comes three times: the supreme light, the light followed by devotees, and the light within that directs (நடத்தும்) the person. Claimed knowledge by recitation misses the last.

title: நடுவு நிலைமை
theme: Standing in the middle (நடுவு நிலைமை): those who stand in the middle gain knowledge, escape hell and become gods, jnanis and even the Lord, and the poet stands with them; the last verse defines them as those who cling to the Lord's feet and name.
structure_note: Three refrain verses on நடுவுநின்றார் (320 to 322), each ending with the poet or the Lord, then a verse (323) saying who they are.

reading: There is no knowledge except for those who stand in the middle; for those who stand in the middle there is no hell; they become good gods, and I too stood in their way.
nuance: நடுவு is the Kural's word for fairness, keeping to no side. In Tirumular it is also traditionally taken as the yogic middle, the poise between the two breaths or the central channel; the verse itself does not decide, and both senses stand.

reading: The good cloud-coloured one stood in the middle; the good reciter of the four Vedas stood in the middle; some who stood in the middle became jnanis; those who stood in the middle became even the good Lord.
nuance: The cloud-coloured one is Vishnu and the reciter of the four Vedas Brahma. நம்பன், the Lord, is a name of Siva; the last line may mean those in the middle become one with him or that the Lord himself stands in the middle.

reading: Some who stood in the middle became jnanis, some gods, some the Lord, and I too stood with those who stood in the middle.
nuance: A near repetition of 320 and 321. The gradation (jnanis, gods, the Lord) suggests different ends for those who keep the same middle.

reading: He alone dissolves all that has come to be; those who stand always holding the Lord's two feet and cling to the holy name of the First are the ones who stand in the middle.
nuance: The verse defines the middle by devotion, not by fairness. மூன்றுநின்றார் is obscure: perhaps standing in the three (thought, word, deed) or at the three times of day. நான்று, hanging, suggests clinging to the name.

title: கள்ளுண்ணாமை
theme: Not drinking liquor (கள்ளுண்ணாமை): liquor and lust confuse, destroy truth and understanding and keep people from knowing soul and bond; the sects that drink for power lose it by forgetting themselves. The drink worth taking is the unceasing nectar of Siva's bliss, reached in samadhi, yoga and the union of Siva and Shakti.
structure_note: Verses alternate between condemning liquor and its sectarian users (324, 326 to 330, 332, 335) and describing the true drink, the தேறல் of Siva's bliss (325, 331, 333, 334, 336). The word தேறல், clear toddy, is turned from liquor to bliss.

reading: As a cow given rice-wash water seeks no pond yet, craving the slop, wastes its body, so those who drink their fill of liquor have left the right order; the true drink is the clear nectar of Siva's bliss.
nuance: கழுநீர் is rice-washing water given to cattle, but can also be the water-lily; the cow image is my best reading of the first two lines. செழுநீர், rich water, describes Siva as the true source of drink.

reading: Those who drink the pure honey, the unceasing nectar of Siva's bliss that comes in the samadhi where the mind melts and becomes Siva, do not leave that bliss, whether standing, sitting or lying down.
nuance: சுத்த மது, pure honey or wine, keeps the vocabulary of drink for bliss. The last line (நித்தல் இருத்தல் கிடத்தல் கீழ்க் காலே) is obscure; I take it as the postures in which the bliss persists, but கீழ்க்கால் may be a yogic term for the lower breath.

reading: Lust and liquor belong to the wretched, and within the sects the great impurity breeds delusion; the mind that goes to the twin feet of the Pure One finds there awareness of the nectar of bliss made of Om.
nuance: போமதி may be 'the departing mind' or 'the mind that goes'; ஓமய is read as ஓம்-மய, made of Om, though it could relate to ஓமம், the fire rite. The verse pairs lust and liquor as the chapter does again in 327 and 330.

reading: Left-hand worshippers drink liquor and die; the lustful drink the liquor of lust and are confused; those of the fire rite know within the inner light; those of the Name draw near that very day.
nuance: வாமத்தோர் are traditionally the followers of the left-hand (Vama) tantra, who use wine in ritual. ஓமத்தோர் may be those of the fire rite or those of Om, and நாமத்தோர் those who repeat the Name; the four groups are ranked.

reading: Those who drink liquor do not ponder the inner truth, do not know soul and bond, do not live in the grace the bountiful Lord gave, and do not reach the Siva-yoga of clear true knowledge; they do not know the meaning.
nuance: பசு பாசம், soul and bond, are two of the three Siddhanta categories, the third being பதி, the Lord, who appears here as the bountiful நாதன். The charge against liquor is that it blocks Siddhanta knowledge, not only good conduct.

reading: Fools in whom the impurity of deluding sects abides, and the great fools who drink deluding liquor, do not discern great maya's delusion or the release from maya; to feel clear inside delusion is itself delusion.
nuance: மயக்கு opens every line. The last line can also be read 'if one grows clear of delusion, delusion ends'; I take it as the drunkard's false clarity.

reading: Liquor bewilders, dulls and destroys truthfulness; drinkers reach only the pleasure of women and embrace them, and do not go forward into the good knowledge that attains unbroken bliss.
nuance: Truthfulness (வாய்மை) is the first casualty named. The two kinds of pleasure, of women and of unbroken bliss, are set side by side through the repeated இயங்கும்.

reading: They do not stay in the place where there is neither night nor day and drink, free of distraction, the nectar of bliss; in the joy of the twin feet where there is neither night nor day, night and day and maya are left behind.
nuance: The place without night and day is traditionally the state beyond the two breaths, the moon and sun channels, or beyond waking and sleep. The last line (இராப்பகல் மாயை இரண்டிடத் தேனே) is obscure: தேன் may be honey or a first-person ending. The corpus notes a parallel in Kandar Alangaram 74, where staying where there is no night and day is called hard.

reading: Sectarians drink liquor seeking power, but the power is destroyed because they forget themselves; real power is to reach Siva-knowledge and join the bliss of truth and knowledge.
nuance: சத்தி is both power and the goddess Shakti, whom some sects worship with wine. சத்திய ஞான ஆனந்தம் echoes the formula of being, knowledge and bliss.

reading: If the Lord of Shakti gives grace, Shakti's grace follows; if Shakti gives grace, his grace follows; when one holds both Shakti and Siva within, truth and the nature of the eight attainments come.
nuance: சத்தன் is the possessor of Shakti, Siva. The mirror-image lines make their grace one. சத்தியம் may be 'truth' or 'it is certain'.

reading: Removing the tattvas and delusion, becoming oneself, removing false tapas, entering true enjoyment, taking the world and leaving it: the nectar of Siva's bliss makes the attainment of supreme bliss.
nuance: தானாகி, becoming oneself, is traditionally the soul knowing itself apart from the tattvas. மெய்த்த சகமுண்டு விட்டு is obscure; I read சகம் as the world.

reading: Yogis who bind the breath taste the nectar of knowledge-bliss from the bright moon and gain the eight attainments; the deluded drink liquor, become fools, fall into infatuation and lose their understanding in intoxication.
nuance: கால் is the breath, and ஒண்மதி the moon, traditionally the place in the head from which yogic nectar is said to flow when the breath is held. The two halves set yogic nectar against liquor, both bringing an altered state, one with siddhis and one without understanding.

reading: Open the spring where the nectar of the inner water wells, think on the guru's lotus feet, draw near in samadhi; then by the water of the channels the good flows with the eye's stream and is seen along the way of the breath.
nuance: நாடிநீர், the water of the channels, கண்ணாறு, the eye's stream, and கால்வழி, the breath's way, are yogic terms whose exact reference I can't fix. நாடி can also be read as 'seeking'. The plain sense is a turn from outer drink to inner nectar under the guru.

title: அகத்தியம்
theme: Agastya (அகத்தியம்): when the world tilted and was failing, the Lord sent Agastya south to set it right, and Agastya, with sages in the west and north, keeps the fire rising so that the light gives plenty everywhere.
source_issues: 338 line 3: மங்கி may be a misreading of அங்கி, which opens lines 1 and 2.

reading: When the gods cried 'our Lord, this world does not stay level, it tilts and is ruined', the Lord said: 'Agastya, fire within the middle, go into the troubled world and stand first there.'
nuance: The verse assumes the legend in which, at Siva's wedding, all beings gathered in the north and the earth tipped, and Agastya was sent south to balance it. நடுவுள அங்கி, the fire in the middle, may be an epithet of Agastya's tapas or a yogic term. Who speaks the second line is not stated.

reading: Agastya, who makes the rising fire grow, with the one in the west who makes the fire rise and the tapas-sage of the north who makes it rise: through them the shining light holds plenty everywhere.
nuance: அங்கி உதயம், the rising of fire, may be the sacrificial fire or the inner fire of yoga. The sages of the west and north are not named. Line 3 begins மங்கி, which may be a misreading of அங்கி.

title: பதிவலியில் வீரட்டம் எட்டு
theme: The eight heroic deeds of the Lord's might (பதிவலியில் வீரட்டம் எட்டு): the slaying of the asura, the punishing of Prajapati and Brahma, the overthrow of Jalandhara, the three cities, the elephant from the fire, Death at Kadavur and Kama at Korukkai. From the three cities on, Tirumular reads the deeds inwardly: the cities are the work of the three impurities, Death is burned in yoga, Kama destroyed by restraint.
structure_note: 339 to 342 tell four deeds as story; 343 turns, calling the literal reading foolish, and 344 to 346 give the remaining deeds with yogic or allegorical senses. The traditional eight sites (Kovalur, Pariyalur, Kandiyur, Virkudi, Athigai, Vazhuvur, Kadavur, Korukkai) are named only in 345 and 346.
source_issues: 342 line 3: பொங்குன்ய் is corrupt, probably for பொங்கும் or பொங்கு; variant யோகிபாற் for யோதிபாற் changes the victim of Jalandhara's attack from a Veda reciter to a yogi.

reading: When the gods begged him, saying that an asura like Andhaka was tormenting all the lives of the world by the power of a boon, the Lord took the high-pointed trident in his hand and killed him.
nuance: Andhaka's slaying is traditionally set at Tirukkovalur. அந்தகன் தன்போல் அசுரன் can be 'an asura like Andhaka' or Andhaka himself; கருத்துறை, in the first line, is unclear.

reading: He struck off the head of Prajapati, who had erred in a matter of killing, and gave it to the fire; then, judging that the stable world needed him, he cut a head and joined it on.
nuance: Prajapati here is taken as Daksha, whose head was burned and replaced, in the legend, with a goat's. கொலையிற் பிழைத்த may mean 'who erred by killing', perhaps the animal of his sacrifice, or 'who escaped death'. The punishment ends in restoration.

reading: The gods who know the feet of the one who pervades everything and bears the great earth so that it stays: in that surging anger Brahma's head was severed, and there he took blood from Achyuta.
nuance: The legend, set at Kandiyur, is that Siva cut off Brahma's fifth head and filled the skull with Vishnu's blood. Whose anger surges (பொங்கும் சினம்) and how the gods in line 2 fit the sentence are unclear.

reading: The First, who mingles everywhere and rises in my heart, when Jalandhara swelled to make war on the reciter of the Vedas, drew a wheel there with his toe in the water.
nuance: In the legend, set at Virkudi, Siva drew a circle with his toe that became the discus which killed Jalandhara. நீர்மையின் is taken as 'in the water' or 'fittingly'. A variant reads யோகிபாற் (against the yogi) for யோதிபாற் (against the reciter).

reading: Fools say the Ancient One, with water in his red matted hair, burned the three cities; the three cities are the work of the three impurities, and who knows that it was these he shot?
nuance: The chapter's turning point: the myth is not denied but read as allegory, the cities being the soul's three bonds (traditionally anava, karma and maya). Tirumular calls the literal reading foolish, not the myth.

reading: At the sacrifice roaring with three fires lit, they did not know who Hara, wearer of the elephant's hide, was; and when the many gods who sought power were there, the killing arose from within that fire.
nuance: The legend, set at Vazhuvur, is that the sages of the Darukavana raised an elephant from their sacrificial fire to kill Siva, who flayed it and wore its hide. The verse names the elephant's hide and the killing from the fire; who the many gods are and who seeks power (சத்தி) is unclear.

reading: Turning the One who blazes at the root opening upward to the upper opening, with the breath joined, he burned Death in the yoga of fire: so Kadavur of the world became good.
nuance: The legend is of Siva kicking Death to save Markandeya at Tirukkadavur. Here it becomes yoga: the fire at the root opening (traditionally the muladhara) is raised by breath (கால்) to the upper opening, and Death is burned. The verse does not name kundalini; the reading is tradition's. கால் is also the leg, so காலுற்றுக் காலனை may pun on the kick.

reading: Making the mind that sat there settle in accord, turning back the way of the linga, destroying the work of Kama: that is the rare yoga of tapas seated at Korukkai.
